items.title: Verity Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
In a piece on how Colleen Hoover became a global best-selling author, one YA fan that was interviewed by the paper suggested it was because she’s “writing for people who don’t like reading.” If that's the case, then one could argue that the film adaptations of her work are for people who don't like cinema.

Now that I've watched all four films inspired by her literary prose — 2024's It Ends with Us, 2025's Regretting You, this year's Reminders of Him, and now Verity — I'm making that case. For these are not adaptations that make any attempt to elevate the middling narratives fumbling around Hoover's novels; I realised this when reading It Ends with Us after suffering through the movie, and I vowed never to read another.

With Verity, I had more hope that it would buck the trend. Divorced from the sentimentality of previous adaptations, this story opens with a meet-cute that’ll give you whiplash. After introducing Anne Hathaway's best-selling author Verity Crawford through interviews with the likes of Gayle King, where she discusses the darkness in her writing, struggling writer Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) enters the chat. Lowen's agent has landed her a meeting with Crawford's publishing house for a mysterious job opportunity, but on the way, she not only witnesses a road accident but is drenched in the blood of the cyclist involved. It's an opener as out there as the one in Meet Joe Black (IYKYK), but it does provide an opportunity for Josh Hartnett's handsome stranger to step in and help clean her up.

In typical Hoover fashion, the pair trauma bond: He tells her he dragged his dead daughter out of a lake, and she says her mother died of cancer the week before. There’s no build up, just some awkward exposition-dumping in a men's toilet. They're soon reunited at the publishing house, where it’s revealed that he's Verity's husband, Jeremy. He and the editors want to commission Lowen to finish his wife's novel series; Verity is in a comatose state after a car accident and cannot speak or move. So, with little deliberation and due to the shoehorned fact that Lowen is also being evicted from her New York apartment, she packs up and moves into the Crawfords' sprawling Vermont home for six months.

There she meets Verity, a shell of her glamorous self wearing a glazed stare. This is one of the few scenes the women share; most of Hathaway's performance is marginalised to interviews on the likes of Hot Ones and the Call Her Daddy podcast, as well as flashbacks layered with sultry voiceovers as Lowen reads Verity's secret autobiography. Every time she picks it up, sentences run across the screen, and often Lowen is superimposed over scenes from the past to try to enliven the act of reading. It doesn't.

What's most infuriating is how long it takes Lowen to finish the text. It’s unbelievable that an author would constantly run away from the autobiography to masturbate and go on a date with Jeremy, given how unflinching Verity's candour is. She reveals juicy details about her marriage and hints that their daughter's death might not have been an accident — how did she not finish it in one sitting? Nothing screams “padding for time” more than this tedious set-up, accomplishing little in the way of ingratiating the viewer with Johnson's "pick me" girl protagonist.

Nothing screams “padding for time” more than this tedious set-up.

Nor does it scratch the surface of who Jeremy actually beyond the one-dimensional trope of a swoon-worthy husband. Screenwriter Nick Antosca, who recently impressed with his adaptation of Cape Fear, hints at some resentment on Jeremy’s part for his wife's success, but the script never probes deeper than in a final act reveal that flings the missing pieces at you in one blink. The best Antosca offers is an examination of the reliability of the narrator, but even that effort is phoned in. Michael Showalter's direction is similarly dull, conveying little of the vision seen in his Oscar-nominated films, The Eyes of Tammy Faye and The Big Sick. Instead, it plods an uneven, uninspiring route into cliché and lazy convention.

That Anne Hathaway has been on an exquisite run of big screen releases from The Odyssey and Mother Mary to The End of Oak Street and The Devil Wears Prada 2 makes this, her last 2026 performance, even more disappointing. What a lead balloon for everyone involved — one that proves a moratorium on Colleen Hoover adaptations is long overdue. To misquote Lady Catherine from Pride and Prejudice: "Are the shades of cinema to be thus polluted?"

items.title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer Review
items.author: Kenny
items.content:
For a series as storied as Star Wars – one brimming with more spacecraft and speeders than George Lucas has beard bristles – it borders on baffling that developer Fuse Games’ Star Wars: Galactic Racer can arrive in 2026 as the first new game of its kind in over two decades. I blame Super Bombad Racing, if only because Gungan isn’t a real language and using a portmanteau of bomb and bad in the title was probably never the perfect pathway to sales success. Galactic Racer, on the other hand, has a range of impressively customisable vehicle classes that expands the hangar well beyond classic podracers, gorgeous course design, and an impressively credible and explorable world outside the on-track action. It’s an eye-catching and rich resurrection of Star Wars racing that’s as fast as it can be surprisingly unforgiving.

Galactic Racer’s main hook is its run-based, roguelite-inspired campaign, which comes with a strict philosophy of no mid-race restarts. It an interesting and genuinely fresh approach that bakes a very real and logical feeling of risk and danger into the action – a feeling that is admittedly absent in racing games with any sort of rewind functionality or unlimited restarts. Yes, you can still pause and, yes, you can still save and come back later – but you otherwise need to live with the consequences of what happens out on the track. It’s a structure that makes the racing tense and meaningful, even if racing over the same landscapes over and over does grow repetitive.

Now This Isn’t Pod Racing

Whether by intent or not, the huge time gap between Galactic Racer and classic Star Wars games like Episode I: Racer and Racer Revenge feels almost mirrored in Fuse Games’ original story. That is, where those games were set in the prequel period, Galactic Racer is set in the aftermath of Return of the Jedi, where the art of podracing is a distant relic of a bygone era. Unsurprisingly, podracing still feature here, and it’s represented incredibly; lightning quick, and with impeccably authentic sound design. However, I’m hesitant to describe specifically how or when it pops up outside of the quickplay modes. Just know that I feel like the Fuse Games crew were paying close attention when Maverick found an F-14 in the heart of enemy territory during the Top Gun sequel, or when Bond retrieved his DB5 in Skyfall. I may be a pretty casual Star Wars fan by most metrics, but I do love stuff that imbues vehicles with a sense of old soul – even fantasy ones. That’s my jam.

For clarity, the bulk of the Galactic Racing League garage consists of landspeeders, speeder bikes, and a new vehicle type called skim speeders. Bikes are fast but fragile, and skim speeders have a podracer-esque ability to bank completely vertically to slice through gaps and turn harder, but landspeeders have proven to be my favourite class. They’re essentially floating cars, and I enjoy their more predictable handling and added durability.

As the mysterious and faceless human racer called Shade, our ultimate goal is to beat the Galactic Racing League’s moaning, arrogant, and entitled heel Kestar Bool in the final head-to-head race. However, for that to happen, we need a suitably fast vehicle. In simple terms, building and piloting a quick one requires a combination of general stat upgrades, performance parts, and various additional perks – from gadgets that can be activated during races to specific bonuses granted to you by allies you accumulate over the course of the story. These are rationed out randomly, or earned, as we progress (and re-progress) through the championship “tours.” I’ve grown to be a particular fan of the autopilot gadget, which is regularly a lifesaver to tackle particularly treacherous stretches of track. The fact that these gadgets are primed just prior to race starts with a series of specific button presses, like pre-flight checks, is a very clever touch that gives waiting on the grid a tangible sense of occasion. The sequence always ends with the final go-ahead to fire your engines, which cough to life and glow harder as you squirt the throttle. It was important to somebody at Fuse Games that we should be able to rev our speeders like hotrodders at a red light, because it looks cool. I love little flourishes like that.

Now, speeders are scrapped between tours, so you’ll need to choose and set-up a new one each time. It’s not a solution I find I’m loving, considering I was never able to establish any real sense of ownership or attachment to a vehicle. Theoretically, you can build a replica of the same-looking vehicle every time – with the same add-on cosmetic parts and the same livery – but you will need to wave goodbye to specific upgrades you might’ve really enjoyed. The more heavily upgraded your previous speeder, the more points you’ll have to spend on pumping up its general stats before you start – but it won’t behave the same as your last one. Not unless you can pick up the same upgrades in your next run, whether by chance reward or spotting them in your mechanic Hibi’s randomised selection. As a roguelite rookie and a traditional racing game meathead, I have to admit I didn’t much like losing powerful upgrades that really suited my racing style to what’s essentially a dice roll, but I do appreciate the novelty of needing to come to grips with something not typical of the usual racers I play.

Tours unfold over three (and later five) planets before culminating in a final knockout event. Failing at any point means you’ll have to start a whole new one over again. This is quite elegantly and thoughtfully implemented, thanks to the racing paddock at each event you can fully explore in third-person. Not only does this build an authentic world around the Galactic Racing League – which in turn crafts a world I feel like I’m inhabiting, rather than just shuffling through menu screens – it lets Fuse Games fill it with characters that can acknowledge your previous failures as you return for another crack at the title. That is, you’re not actually , or simply being scrubbed back in time until you get it right – time keeps moving forward and you just need to keep racing until you emerge victorious. The story is split into three distinct acts, so note that messing up in the third act means you’ll just need to take another run at the third act. That is, it doesn’t send us all the way back to the initial League qualification phase, and for that I’m grateful.

However, Galactic Racer’s core weakness is that it unfortunately doesn’t feature enough planets to avoid feeling overly repetitive. While I’m conscious a roguelite structure brings with it an expectation of a certain level of repetition, it does become fairly tedious slogging through its small list of repeating planets over successive attempts. The specific circuits used, the order of event types, and how they branch over the span of a championship shuffled from tour to tour. There are reverse layouts for the tracks, too. However, the backdrops are nonetheless always the same. Having a couple more planets that could’ve been swapped in and out would’ve gone a long way in reducing the fatigue that quickly sets in after several runs through the same locations.

It is a fantastically realised array of planets, though, and the details of the track environments are as excellent as they are varied. Jakku, for instance, has routes traced through its immense graveyard of war wreckage – swinging from wide open blasts across debris-covered dunes one moment, to cramped sections of makeshift tunnels formed by half-destroyed spacecraft the next. Crait is characterised by sprawling caves and its flat, salt-covered surface – which speeders whip up to expose the red mineral beneath. Lantaana is covered in dense forest linked by lava tubes, and Sentinel I is a toxic wasteland where racers must negotiate narrow causeways over acidic pools.

Each planet and track has its own set of properties that can help you or harm you, depending on how you race and the upgrades you’ve applied. Perhaps my favourite example of this dynamic is Ando Prime, an entirely frozen planet, where heating tubes have been dropped sporadically around the circuits. Passing through these will thaw out the frozen control surfaces that numb your steering inputs, but staying of these hot boxes allows you to run your delicate ramjet for much longer before it catastrophically burns out. It’s a racer that essentially never stops asking you questions.

On the topic of burning out, it’d be massively remiss of me not to mention how much I adore the Burnout-inspired takedowns that Galactic Racer actively encourages, with speeders on the wrong side of a hefty slam being speared into trackside obstacles and splintering into thousands of shards. Not only are they incentivised with a slow-motion takedown camera, which swings back to soak in the spectacle, but they can be factored into the upgrade system. Any time I spot it on a run, I always opt to grab the upgrade that replenishes my speeder’s battery for each successful takedown – since doing so gives me more bursts of my autopilot ability.

Perhaps what I love most of all is how much Galactic Racer surprisingly reminded me of a sci-fi MotorStorm.

But while the Burnout connection is strong (and hardly surprising considering the roots of Fuse Games’ founders reach back to Burnout creator Criterion Games), perhaps what I love most of all is how much Galactic Racer surprisingly reminded me of a sci-fi MotorStorm. That is, the often wide tracks full of natural obstacles and multiple routes, the multi-class nature of the grid, and the fact that holding onto that ramjet boost a fraction too long results in a fiery and rapid unscheduled disassembly. Funnily enough, just like the original MotorStorm, Galactic Racer also has no splitscreen multiplayer. 12-player online racing (or eight, for podracers) has a six-event championship structure that works a little like a shortened version of the singleplayer tours (where your upgraded vehicle is discarded after the finale) – but that’s for a different sort of player than me.

items.title: HBO's War Season 1 Premiere Review and Recap
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Full spoilers follow for the season premiere of War.

HBO’s slick new legal drama War will almost certainly be its next big watercooler show, and deservedly so, as it’s a sharply written, deftly paced, and well-acted trashy delight.

The Season 1 premiere quickly establishes rival London law firms Cathcarts & Sons and Taylor & Byrne and their respective clients: social media mogul Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) and his movie star wife Carla Duval (Sienna Miller). Their long, now loveless marriage is basically over. So that means a very expensive and very public divorce will inevitably follow.

Carla not only wants out of the marriage, but she also wants to take Morgan’s fortune with her. But their pre-nuptial agreement is designed to keep Morgan bulletproof — provided he has lived up to his end of their bargain. He hasn’t. He’s been unfaithful to her before but this time Carla is armed with photographic evidence thanks to .

Carla assures her lawyers she didn’t enlist her younger actress friend to sleep with Morgan but that doesn’t ring true. Her lawyers Serena Byrne (Phoebe Fox) and Nicholas Taylor (James McArdle), partners in both the firm and romantically, don’t like Carla’s underhandedness as it could be bad optics. Carla wants to file for divorce first but she and Taylor & Byrne are unaware that Morgan and his lawyers at Cathcarts have already deduced that she’s poised to file.

Beatrice “Queen Bea” Ubosi (Nina Sosanya) and St John Smallwood (Pip Torrens), Serena and Nicholas’ counterparts at Cathcarts, fire the first shot in this war by serving Carla divorce papers on the red carpet at the premiere of her new movie, a savage move reminiscent of Olivia Wilde being served onstage at CinemaCon. And Carla then has to smile for the cameras with Morgan at her side?! Ouch.

The episode’s biggest surprise, however, is saved for when we learn that the ambitious, overconfident young lawyer Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux) – newly hired by Taylor & Byrne specifically to work on Carla’s divorce – is, in fact, a mole working for Cathcarts. For the entire episode, we follow Johnny’s desperate search for a job at a law firm, so the reveal that he’s going to be the show’s equivalent of Matt Damon in The Departed is a fun twist.

Still, as a scrappy, lower class guy trying to make his way up the social ladder, Johnny is sympathetic — for now. Like Charlie Sheen’s character in Wall Street, the question remains just how much of his soul he’s willing to sell to succeed and how many personal relationships Johnny may destroy in the process. It’s a testament to the writing and to Renaux’s nuanced performance that the viewer remains invested in Johnny even when his arrogance gets the better of him.

War is impeccably acted across the board by an ensemble cast filled with familiar UK character actors playing the respective firms’ legal teams. As for the leads, West finds some sad-sack sympathy in his tech bro mogul, while Miller imbues Carla with a steely resolve that suggests she’d have been a natural fit in the boardroom had she not pursued acting. They’re only in one sequence together this episode but it’s rife with tension.

Showrunner George Kay’s finely tuned script is as darkly funny as it is sad in its portrait of the wounded (if not outright lost) humanity of its many characters, people who may not want to be this nasty but, well, that’s what you’re paid for, luv. I can’t wait to see what these posh bastards do next.

items.title: We Build LEGO SpongeBob SquarePants Bikini Bottom: a F.U.N. Build for Nostalgic Adults
items.author: Matthew Adler
items.content:
LEGO SpongeBob SquarePants: Bikini Bottom (available now exclusively from the LEGO Store) is the first new SpongeBob-themed set since 2012, and the first designed for adults with an 18+ age rating. It includes plenty of references and gags from the series, making it an excellent set for longtime fans to put together.

The original set featuring the iconic homes and denizens of Bikini Bottom released in 2006, composed of just 579 pieces, and included a rather horrifying Squidward minifigure. Now, 20 years later, the set is much larger and has been completely reimagined for an older audience. At 1,794 pieces, more than three times the number of the original, this is also the largest LEGO SpongeBob SquarePants set released .

The contents of the massive box are split across 14 bags. This is the second set I've built that uses LEGO's new eco-friendly packaging, which replaces the transparent polyethylene bags with paper bags, an initiative that began back in 2021. While I appreciate the positive environmental impact these new bags promise, I've found that they are prone to having small pieces get stuck in the seams. If you're building a set that includes these new bags, be sure to double-check each one if you're potentially missing a piece.

One aspect I really like about this set is just how good the minifigs look. Each one has been redesigned from the previous iterations, with more accurate colors and improved moldings. SpongeBob, in particular, looks great. The color is spot-on, and he finally has a proper pair of printed pants instead of looking like he's standing on a pair of brown stilts. SpongeBob also comes with his trusty jellyfish net.

Patrick's minifig received a substantial redesign compared to his originals as his head and stomach are now one large piece that fit over the torso like a sort-of reverse cape that more accurately depicts his food-loving physique. He even comes with one of his favorite junk foods – a Neopolitan ice cream cone.

Squidward got the biggest glow-up compared to his original minifig. Although later iterations fixed this by giving him a proper head mold, the version included in this set features a more accurate face, improved coloring, and little tentacles printed on the feet.

While not minifigs per se, the set also comes with a buildable DoodleBob (complete with the Magic Pencil) and a buildable Gary the Snail, although it hasn't changed much from early LEGO iterations aside from having better coloring. He doesn't have eyes, though.

This set is divided into two instruction books, with the first book covering Patrick and Squidward's houses, and the second book dedicated entirely to SpongeBob's famous "Pineapple Under the Sea," which employs some unique tactics to get its shape – more on that later. There are also a number of smaller builds to round out the scenery, including the crooked Bikini Bottom sign, a Boatmobile, SpongeBob's Bubblestand, and small diorama of the Jellyfish Fields, with a small rotating platter to make the jellyfish swim around.

Patrick's house doesn't take long to put together, as all of its contents fit in a single bag. After all, it is just a large rock covering a hole in the ground. Thankfully, LEGO didn't just stop there. The lid of Patrick's house can be opened to reveal all of his sand furniture, including his chair, lamp, rug, and CRT TV. It even includes a space for him to "sleep" under the lid.

Squidward's house, split across six bags, is a little more involved to assemble as it's comprised of four floors: the bottom floor which features his clarinet and music sheet; the second floor with his canopy bed; and the third floor bathroom, complete with his toilet, shower, and bubble bath. There's also a shower curtain with what appears to be a silhouette of SpongeBob hiding behind it - a reference to the episode "Squid's Day Off," where Squidward becomes paranoid after leaving SpongeBob in charge of the Krusty Krab. Finally, the top floor of the house features Squidward's tanning bed that he frequently sets up in front of his house, along with a mirror and a flower-topped cocktail drink.

The interior of the house repurposes some LEGO pieces in interesting ways, such as a pink-colored crown as a sea anemone plant and an upside down cupcake piece as the lampshades for Squidward's nightstands.

LEGO absolutely nailed the exterior of Squidward's house. The dark blue pieces look fantastic, and the chunky geometry of the large nose, ears, and thick brow come through great. The window "eyes" are also a unique printed piece, of which this set has a surprising amount. I was pleased to find only two small sticker sheets overall.

The highlight of this set is undoubtedly SpongeBob's pineapple house, though, which comes together across the remaining seven bags. The bottom floor features plenty of references to the show, including a hidden Mermaid Man and Barnacle Boy Easter egg inside the TV set, the shellphone, the photo of Gary on the wall, and even SpongeBob's "friends" Penny, Chip, and Used Napkin.

Upstairs, SpongeBob's bedroom includes his bed, complete with ladder and diving board, of course, as well as his alarm clock and Gary's dessert in the corner. Don't worry, ,

The designers at LEGO took a very interesting approach to recreate the rounded nature of the pineapple's exterior and its criss-crossed diamond pattern. Each one of the pinapple panels is attached to a rigid internal frame built out of Technics pieces, allowing them to sit on an angle and pivot a bit to create the rounded look. Individual panels are attached to the exterior, leaving a small gap around the edges to make the diamond pattern. While they don't fit together perfectly, the overall shape and finished house looks fantastic.

Finally bringing all three houses together to recreate the Bikini Bottom landscape is a blast. Each of the bases can be connected to save space, or you can display them all freely. There's so much character to this set with endless scenes that can be recreated that it's a must-have for SpongeBob SquarePants fans.

LEGO SpongeBob SquarePants: Bikini Bottom, Set #11386, retails for $219.99 and is composed of 1,794 pieces. It is available to purchase exclusively from the LEGO Store.

Matthew Adler has written for IGN since 2019 covering all things gaming, tech, tabletop games, and more. You can follow him on the site formerly known as Twitter

items.title: Ghost of Yotei DLC Review – Echoes of Sekigahara and Most Wanted
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
Looking to the past to expand on a current game is a pretty common avenue for post-launch content, and developer Sucker Punch does this in more ways than one for Ghost of Yotei. Echoes of Sekigahara weaves in flashbacks from lead character Atsu's life for a brief yet effective questline woven into the middle of the base game. Alongside that is the new Most Wanted mode, which introduces grueling run-based combat challenges – a major highlight of which is that Ghost of Tsushima's Jin Sakai is a playable character, with all of his original mechanics intact. Together, these additions deliver more of what the series is so good at: lethal, precise ronin combat and beautiful landscapes for its violent drama. They're not breaking any new ground, but they distill what made Ghost of Yotei great to begin with.

First thing you need to know is that both Echoes of Sekigahara and Most Wanted are packaged together in the newly minted Ghost of Yotei: Complete Edition, and if you already own the base game, it's a $15 upgrade through the PlayStation store. You'll need to have progressed roughly 10 hours into the original story (where you've taken down a handful of the Yotei Six) in order to initiate a bounty called "Nagato, the Handsome" and access Echoes of Sekigahara, while Most Wanted is available from the main menu right off the bat. They're two very distinct things, so I'll be looking at them separately, but just know that both are worthwhile in their own right.

One of my favorite aspects of Yotei in comparison to Tsushima was the way Atsu contrasted with Jin – she's brash and fueled by vengeance, giving her revenge tale a more personal edge. Echoes of Sekigahara further emphasizes this by exploring her more intimate side, introducing an old flame named Nagato – he's known across the land of Ezo as "The Handsome" because, well, he is a good looking dude, not gonna lie. After accepting a bounty with his name on it, you're ushered into an all-new region on the map known as Ashoro Foothills with its own questline and set of open-world activities in the same vein as the base game, but condensed for a tight seven-to-eight hours of new content.

The impetus for the quest is to cut off resources to Lord Saito's army (the villain of the main story) and to take down a ravenous faction called The Vipers and multiple big-bads vying to replace The Snake – the member of the Yotei Six who Atsu kills at the very start. Atsu gradually unravels Nagato's motives for pursuing these objectives alongside her while confronting him about what happened between them three years ago. They'd been high-ranking comrades on the frontlines of the tide-turning Battle of Sekigahara, and short playable flashbacks throughout this new questline give insight into their past; a budding romance and the interpersonal struggles of mixing business and pleasure. Like Ghost of Yotei itself, the story is a bit predictable, but even when you can see what's coming, it's still captivating for it's told. With Nagato being a sly trooper and Atsu constantly balancing her emotions and pragmatism, the way their personalities clash and harmonize is really well done.

Nagato accompanies Atsu on most of the main missions, and that comes with the perk of having him target a separate enemy whenever you aim your bow. It makes for sweet double kills from a distance and a nice tool to have in your belt during this DLC’s frequent stealth scenarios. Otherwise, he'll support you in fights without much of an effect, if only to occupy enemies and take some of the heat off you. The main addition to Atsu's arsenal are the disposable Massive Weapons – some heavier enemies drop these and you can find them on weapon racks in combat arenas. They don't really change up the already fantastic dynamic of Yotei's rock-paper-scissors weapon mechanics, but I can't deny that it's satisfying to just swing a big-ass club or axe that not even fully armored samurai twice my size can block.

There are quite a few walk-and-talk sequences combined with platforming/cliff-scaling, which I liked quite a bit because I was fairly invested in their banter. Yotei's brand of Uncharted-style climbing has a certain weight I really enjoy as well, and whether Atsu had to do this alone or with Nagato, I was treated to some of the most gorgeous vistas in all of video games. It reminded me of how impressive Ghost of Yotei looks; the Kurosawa imitation in cutscenes is still prominent, of course, but the way colors pop across landscapes, leaves get swept in the wind, and backdrops give a sense of scale are integral to this series. Your first impression of Ashoro Foothills may be that it's a desolate plains ravaged by warlords and bandits, but it's still home to beautiful views you wouldn't get from other technical powerhouses.

With Nagato being a sly trooper and Atsu constantly balancing her emotions, their personalities clash and harmonize really well.

Sidequests fill out the new region and may seem like just your standard fare of checklist-y objectives where you fight a mob of bandits or opportunistic samurai to save villagers. But I appreciate how they at least roll into a bigger idea of rebuilding and defending a region that's mostly been forgotten about and left to fend for itself. There's one particular questline that delves into The Snake's family business – it's a small, but satisfying way to frame Atsu's version of revenge to circumvent the "you're just as bad as the bad guy" trope.

Echoes of Sekigahara as a whole is well-rounded in that it's an extension of Yotei's better parts while doing enough to make it feel like I learned something important about Atsu as a character. And it's a damn fine excuse for more of the already excellent combat, whether it be chaining assassinations or hitting a perfect parry before striking down a foe as I'm on the brink of death. It's definitely a case where more of a good thing isn't bad at all.

I had high praise for the deadly, incisive combat in my original review for Ghost of Yotei, and the new Most Wanted mode offers up more of that hand over fist. Here, you have six different bounties centered around the Yotei Six villains, and you must survive several rounds against waves of enemies and minibosses in order to make it to them. You have to take down each bounty target in one attempt and they get progressively harder. No stealth or exploration, just straight combat, and that rules.

The four hunters you can choose to play as – Atsu, Oyuki, Nagato, or Jin Sakai – act as combat classes who have different weapon loadouts. Everyone gets a katana, but by default Atsu comes with dual katanas, a bow, and a quickfire pistol while Oyuki comes with the kusarigama, a musket, and kunai, as examples. The same rock-paper-scissors weapon dynamic still exists so overcoming certain enemies you may not have a direct answer for pushes you to get a little creative and make use of projectiles, weapon drops, and throwables.

Waves can get overwhelming quickly as well since they'll send mobs at you in a way story-based encounters never did. This was frustrating at first, but instead of brute forcing it, I began to think more tactically and make use of every tool I had. Smoke bombs and fire bombs were clutch for crowd control, archers in the distance needed to be taken out immediately, and the kusarigama's charge combo kept groups at bay. I knew this from the base game, but the stakes felt higher here, so assessing situations and adapting became just as (if not more) important as nailing perfect dodges and parries.

After a few rounds, you can choose one perk from a random assortment of three for just that run. These can be additional weapons that your selected hunter doesn't come with, or boons that range from “nice to have” to a major advantage if you form a build around them. Things like inflicting poison, setting a foe on fire after a number of hits from a certain weapon, or causing a bomb to go off from killed enemies. Two of my favorites were one that automatically activated a free smoke bomb after landing a headshot on marked targets, and another that inflicted fear on surrounding enemies after a perfect parry. These helped tremendously when handling tough bosses or mobs that seemed insurmountable, and little eureka moments where the right decision and good execution came together made me see Yotei's combat in a new light.

Playing as Jin again was refreshing, too, because he controls like he did in Tsushima with his different stances being suited for going up against certain enemy weapon types. Of course, that was still the overarching basis for Yotei, but he feels distinct thanks to his nimble movement between forms, using one katana and the strong attack combos that are his alone (the sticky bombs he packs are also the best quickfire weapon). That’s a nice nod to Tsushima, preserving its specific mechanics and fitting them into Most Wanted's combat gauntlets.

Each of the bounties take place in existing points of interest from the story's open world, drawing from a random assortment of villages and encampments. The bosses are recycled from the campaign as well, so you're not going to see anything entirely new in Most Wanted. That said, the way they're remixed and formatted as run-based challenges for do-or-die situations is enough to create a new kind of tension and let the combat system itself sing again.

The new Most Wanted mode offers up more deadly, incisive combat hand over fist, and that rules.

However, throwing a higher volume of combatants at you shows some limitations – specifically, targeting. Since the series doesn't use a deliberate lock-on system (which is largely for the better), it relies on magnetizing you to the closest enemy or the one your character is facing. Sometimes it confuses one for the other and may pull you toward enemies you didn't intend to attack. For example, I'd perfect parry an enemy I'm facing which would push them back slightly, and of course I'd want to follow up with a combo, right? Well, if another enemy behind me or to the side is just close enough, it'd make me start whaling on them instead, wasting an opportunity to get a kill from a parry. Sometimes it's not that big of a deal and I would just reset and lock back in, but the moments in which it's consequential are undeniably frustrating, especially in final boss fights where they summon mobs to join them. Every move counts, and if that leaves me open to surrounding enemies or spoils a chance to bounce back, long effortful runs can end in disappointment.

Thankfully, blips like this are infrequent so as to not overshadow everything else Yotei's combat system does so well. I was surprised by how much time and effort I put into Most Wanted and how invested I was in finishing bounties, with that familiar voice in my head saying, "just one more run." It's rewarding enough to stick with and highlights what Sucker Punch had built when the series started.

items.title: South Park Season 29, Episode 2 Review & Recap: 'Billionaire Weenietown'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for South Park Season 29, Episode 2!

Following a season premiere that felt like a throwback to a more classic incarnation of South Park, the series pivots in Episode 2 with a more topical approach. As the title suggests, "Billionaire Weenietown" is all about skewering the billionaire class, specifically the fact that we can't seem to escape their attention-seeking, data center-building ways. It's a fine episode, but one that's mostly carried by the ever-dependable Butters and his family.

The conflict this week comes as Butters finds he can no longer enjoy his precious Dr. Pimple Popper videos. South America has become infested with billionaires who have built a power-hungry new data center literally in Butters' backyard. And he's not going to stand for it one minute longer.

Again, I think the Stotch family storyline in this episode works a bit better than the Weenietown half of things. There's certainly a fun novelty in seeing just how literally this episode takes the whole "Billionaire Weenietown" concept. There's never not some fun to be had in watching a bunch of talking penises bicker with each other and go on The Joe Rogan Experience. It's a way for the series to make fun of the Elon Musks and Mark Zuckerbergs of the world without directly including them.

But as is sometimes the case on this show, the shelf life of that particular gag is limited. This episode leans a bit too hard on the "billionaires are dorks who think everyone wants to hear their opinions" joke when, frankly, there are a lot more reasons to make fun of them besides. The resolution to the Weenietown conflict is also a bit too simple and abrupt for my liking. That said, I'm curious to see if the writers find ways of integrating the remaining Billionaire Weenies into the remainder of Season 29. Hopefully they don't become the new Member Berries...

But it's hard to muster too much criticism for an episode that gives us such a concentrated dose of Butters. If anything, this normally plucky, innocent character is even more entertaining when he's pushed over the edge. Angry Butters is a good Butters, and that anger really carries the day here. Whether it's his tantrum in the classroom or his interactions with the pest control guy, Butters is a real hoot here. Who can't empathize with his righteous anger at this point?

Well, his parents sure can't. Butters' crusade tees up a hilarious subplot where Steve and Linda Stotch fear their precious baby boy has contracted "libtardedness." That subplot serves as a terrific sendup of the anti-vax movement and a certain brand of self-educated, Joe Rogan-loving know-it-all. With the two parents having a complete meltdown while Butters is off doing his own thing, this episode feels like a direct callback to 2001's "Butters' Very Own Episode." That formula still works very well. Though this subplot does sort of drop off before the episode's end. I was expecting some sort of payoff to the FBI call that never comes. Maybe that's a seed for another day?

Finally, I can't not mention the ending. After going nearly two full episodes without roasting Donald Trump directly, the series turns all of its wrath back his way with another goofy deepfake sequence. It's an amusing way to cap off this episode. Coming off of such a Trump-heavy Season 27 and 28, I wouldn't necessarily mind if the show limited itself to these occasional roasts rather than making him a central character again. We'll just have to see what direction Season 29 takes as we get closer to November and the all-important release of GTA.

items.title: Carrie Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
It’s easy to forget that for all the haunted hotels, dark towers, cursed cemeteries, society-ending viruses, killer clowns, and various and sundry things that go bump in the night that Stephen King has subjected us to, the author’s half-century grip on the horror genre started with a telekinetic teenage girl named Carrie White. Carrie’s cautionary tale of bullying has been adapted and sequelized numerous times, and Kimberly Peirce’s 2013 film even beat Mike Flanagan to the punch by first pulling Carrie into the 21st century. But, as is often the case when Flanagan brings King to the screen, Carrie successfully celebrates what makes the novel so relevant 52 years after its first publication by evolving with the times and palpably deepening King’s characters.

The opening moments of the premiere treat Carrie’s story with a Shakespearean level of reverence, with a Greek chorus of doc-style talking heads giving an overview of the story’s well-known beats that led to that fateful prom night. Inviting a closer look at all angles of that story is the dramatic thrust of Carrie, and the series sets itself up well for that effort by structuring itself as a teen drama in the vein of Pretty Little Liars or Riverdale. Carrie is an epistolary novel which heavily relies on interviews with the survivors of the prom night massacre and documentary evidence to tell Carrie’s story, and the series replicates that fractured perspective of the events by quickly setting up different groups of characters tied to Carrie as focal points for the narrative to jump around to.

Flanagan and his team are broadly successful in adapting the story and themes already present in King’s novel to the teen drama format. Carrie’s not a plot-heavy book, and the series compensates for that by spending more time on exploring how everyone is processing the events as they play out, and how the evolving interpersonal and public relations crises are picking at scabs at the back of the minds of characters like Carrie’s teacher Rita Desjardin (Amber Midthunder) and Principal Grayle (Matthew Lillard). The extra time and scope afforded to the story is a rising tide that lifts all boats, even if that format does occasionally leave room for some overwrought stylistic or dramatic choices. There are a few too many on-the-nose dream pop needle drops with lyrics that explain what the action of a given scene has already communicated just fine.

Flanagan and his team are broadly successful in adapting the story and themes already present in King’s novel to the teen drama format.

Carrie is not one of Stephen King’s strongest characters on the page - that epistolary style of the novel leaves Carrie often feeling a little decentralized from her own story - but that problem doesn’t persist into the TV series. The Carrie series is unquestionably successful in its most important effort: putting the plight of its two central characters, Carrie and Margaret White, into a modern context. As Carrie, Summer H. Howell is totally magnetic from her first moments onscreen. Carrie’s wide-eyed enthusiasm for integrating with the outside world is contagious, even as her first day with classmates like good-natured Sue Snell (Siena Agudong) and mean girl Chris Hargensen (Alison Thornton) proves to be overwhelming. Howell’s accommodating and empathetic energy, even in the face of how poorly Carrie’s treated by the world, is a well of positivity and light that Flanagan and his team of directors - Kate Siegel, Axelle Carolyn, Kyra Sedgwick and Hiromi Kamata - continually put to the test across not just the classic challenges from her story, but the new ones afforded by the present-day setting. As Carrie becomes more self-assertive and is then tempted towards darkness, Howell’s work is even more impressive, and the writing does a good job giving her the space to take Carrie down more intense lanes without losing sight of the precocious girl she is at heart.

Carrie getting pelted with tampons in the shower by a gang of girls led by Chris Hargensen while she gets her first period is bad enough, but the show follows that event to its next logical permutation in 2026: what happens when video of that kind of horrific bullying makes its way onto social media in the form of a meme account run by Chris, “CarrieRed.” The viral spread of the “CarrieRed” account, and the resulting fallout, is a reliable kettle the show keeps on the boil throughout the season. With that in mind, despite its supernatural trappings, much of the show’s horror is internal and existential. There are surely scares, but by and large, Carrie is content to let the experience of being a teenage girl be its own engine of horror.

Of course, Carrie’s reaction to being so callously treated by people she just wanted to be friends with is paramount, but the show takes pains to keep Sue and Chris’s experiences of these in focus as the two social poles between which Carrie is being pulled. Both Siena Agudong and Alison Thornton are good in their roles, but with Sue being a naturally decent person who usually makes the right decision, it’s Thornton’s volatile Chris that winds up with more exciting material, especially given how Flanagan and company use her own complicated circumstances at home to serve as a foil to Carrie’s. Chris’ life is falling apart, with an estranged mom and a jerk father whose poor planning leaves her freshman year of college in jeopardy, and despite the fathomless cruelty that Chris inflicts on Carrie, the writing finds grace for Chris by making clear that there are plenty of ways that poor parenting can leave a girl ill-equipped to navigate the trials of growing up in 2026.

Carrie’s relationship to the events of the plot are largely unchanged from the novel, so it’s Samantha Sloyan’s Margaret White, Carrie’s mother, who winds up as the character with the most worthwhile overhaul here. Margaret White is one of the most famous religious zealots of horror fiction, but this series explores the roots of that fundamentalism in a much more nuanced way, a mission statement the series makes right off the bat with a canny alteration to the book’s inciting incident.

The death of Ralph White, Margaret’s husband, still leads to the authorities discovering Carrie’s shut-in conditions back at home but, this time, the cops discover both Carrie Margaret holed up in the family prayer closet, where sinners in this house are sent to repent. The way Ralph looms as a specter over their home even after his death makes it clear as the season continues that Margaret’s fervent attempts at protecting her daughter from the outside world are rooted in the ways her relationship to her ultra-right wing husband warped her own worldview. Margaret sees herself as a holy warrior, and is there no more ungodly battlefield in that war than the town square of social media, especially with her daughter being savaged there on a daily basis?

Samantha Sloyan, a frequent Flanagan collaborator, is perfectly cast as Margaret, with the actress’s intensity and openness each a perfect fit for the character’s megalomania and genuine love for Carrie. Sloyan is at her best taking that holy warrior energy toe-to-toe with those she sees as adversaries at the school, like Principal Grayle, who are mostly doing their best to balance doing right by Carrie with the institutional loopholes that leave them hamstrung in those efforts. How willing others in the town of Chamberlain seem to be to cosign Margaret’s style of guardianship call attention to her pridefulness in ways that don’t let her off the hook from being responsible for her choices, but do wonders for pointing out how prevalent the tendency to be “holier than thou” really is these days.

What shakiness is present in how Carrie is expanded out to eight episodes of TV comes from a side plot and characters that Flanagan and the writers have created to underline Carrie’s significance to the wider Kingverse. Their presence does at least make sense, given how freely the Carrie novel acknowledges the presence of other characters with the “TK gene” out in the world. Flanagan uses one character in particular to give structure to each episode, most beginning with her narration about the story of another gifted girl or woman out in the world. It’s during these vignettes that the series’ writing is at its least subtle, lacking enough variety in how they speak to the way Carrie represents all disenfranchised women to keep them from feeling a little repetitious by the season’s end.

The varying mileage these additional plot elements get is perhaps best represented in the presence of another brand-new character, Emaline (Thalia Dudek). Emaline is another new student at Ewen High who befriends Carrie and encourages her to take a more active stance against her antagonists but, as written, Emaline’s function in the story winds up being a little too one-note for a little too long to feel like a necessary invention. The Carrie series folds in this supporting roster of characters sparingly, but their presence does call for the show’s focus to occasionally drift, especially as things start heating up going into the finale.

items.title: Gears of War: E-Day Review
items.author: Kenny
items.content:
: This review currently only covers Gears of War: E-Day's story campaign, as that’s all reviewers were given access to ahead of release. It will be updated with a finalized score and multiplayer impressions once we spend some time with the Versus and Horde Siege modes.

To the casual observer, Gears of War has always been a heavy-metal third-person cover shooter about a bunch of meatheads with chainsaws attached to their guns fighting aliens. But what Gears fans know all too well is that the real secret to the series’s two decades of success isn’t the killer graphics, the smart cover mechanics, or the gloriously gratuitous gore – although those things are all certainly significant parts of the recipe. It’s the heart. Marcus and Dom’s brotherhood. JD or Del’s sacrifice (depending on what you chose to do in Gears 5). Dom’s relentless love for Maria. And so my biggest question heading into Gears of War: E-Day, a prequel to the first game set 14 years prior on the day the Locust emerged from underneath the planet Sera, was how it would hang onto that heart when we already knew our armor-clad bros would definitely be alive by the end. I’m thrilled to say that E-Day carries its own satisfying emotional weight, with additional welcomed backstory for Marcus and Dom leading the way – oh, and the action is pretty top-notch, too.

E-Day begins with our Coalition of Ordered Government (COG) heroes, Marcus Fenix and Dominic Santiago, completing a ceremonial tour to honor their service in the finally-ended 79-year Pendulum Wars. We get glimpses of how each of them is reckoning with the end of the only thing they’ve ever known: Marcus is ready to re-enlist and hoping Dom will join him, while Dom is ready to go home to his wife Maria and their two young children, who are growing up without him. Of course, things quickly go to Hell – or rather, Hell comes up to them. Gears of War: E-Day does an excellent job of conveying both the uncertainty and the horror of what’s happening to these characters, even when we as players know exactly what’s going on.

By happenstance, Marcus and Dom get unofficially paired up with ex-Gear Mags Carter and rookie Gear Lucas Reyes, who happen to be at the same bar when the Locust tremors begin, before the quartet officially becomes Bravo Squad once the COG starts organizing its defenses. E-Day deserves a lot of credit here: In a prequel like this where you’re already attached to the leads, it would be easy for Carter and Reyes to be throwaway side characters who exist only to further the stories of our two well-known heroes. But E-Day makes time for your lesser-known Bravo squadmates, dedicating entire meaningful and enjoyable sections to establishing them in this world and getting you to care about them.

The unfolding nightmare of E-Day is reflected in both the types of Locust monsters you face as the campaign progresses as well as the sorts of weapons you’ll need to put them back in the ground. Easily-dispatched Wretches and run-of-the-mill, Hammerburst-wielding Drones are on the front lines as Bravo Squad wonders what the hell it’s up against in the invasion’s opening hours. You’ll take them down with Gears of War staples like the Gnasher shotgun and Lancer, both the bayonet-clad original version and the prototype of the chainsaw-equipped revision. Yes, you’ll get your hands on Gears’s most famous firearm pretty early, and you even get to witness its fun little origin story.

E-Day makes time for your lesser-known squadmates and gets you to care.

But as you move through the first hours of the Locust invasion, Bravo Squad is continually confused and terrified at the increasingly deadly horrors trying to kill them. The monster menagerie is, naturally, a mix of foes you have and haven’t seen before in other Gears of War games, and the battles get steadily more white-knuckle as you make your way through the five-act story. Giant, frog-like hopping freaks that arc multi-gallon acidic loogies at you. Heavies that come in multiple varieties, most menacingly the one that fires a medium-range Gorehook – a hook on a chain that will typically down you in one hit.

On that note, one of my few complaints about Gears of War: E-Day is related to the down-but-not-out situations you’ll find yourself in throughout the campaign. When, not if, you get downed, your allies will occasionally be standing right next to you and not revive you. In fairness, it wasn’t a constant occurrence, but there were numerous times throughout my 15-18 hour first playthrough when I got stomped to death by a Locust heavy because one of my buddies either stood next to me and didn’t get me up, ran off and left me for dead, or never even got over to me as I mashed the X button to cling to life for a while. The immediate solution for this is to play through E-Day in four-player online co-op (two-player split-screen is the limit on a single Xbox), but I sure hope a patch resolves this inconsistent AI behavior sooner rather than later as well.

As with the Locust enemies, E-Day’s weapons are a mix of old and new, and my goodness do I love them. Every weapon has a unique purpose to suit a particular combat strategy. And man, it still feels to blast a Locust Heavy to bits with the Gnasher shotgun, cut a Drone into pieces with the Lancer Prototype’s chainsaw attachment, or explode a Locust sniper’s head with a scoped-Longshot kill. But there’s so much more in there beyond those Gears classics. The Breechshot, first introduced in the often-forgotten Gears of War: Judgment, ended up being one of my go-tos the longer the campaign went on, as it offered solid range and stopping power without being as cumbersome as something like the Longshot sniper rifle.

But there are a lot of weapons I’d give shoutouts to as well, like the Incinerator, which shotgun-blasts a burst of flesh-melting Imulsion; the Ripper, which is basically the Gears-universe equivalent of a SAW; and the ol’ favorite Torque Bow, which has a hell of a windup but then unleashes an explosive arrow at your target. I loved the weapon complement here, as well as the options that deep roster of firearms afforded me in some of the campaign’s later battles.

And it’s not just that all of these weapons are fun to use in the right situation. They can also all be modified and upgraded through E-Day’s new Weapon Mod and Tactical Gear system. You’ll encounter dozens of yellow Hard Cases lightly hidden throughout the world for you to find. Each contains a mod for one weapon or another, such as accuracy enhancers, scopes, or clip extenders. Completing optional secondary objectives around the major industrial city of Kalona where E-Day takes place also grants these same rewards. Each weapon has four mod slots, which you’ll unlock as you go, and I found myself constantly tweaking each weapon to find the right mix of add-ons that suited my playstyle. As such, I was plenty motivated to find every Hard Case I could and complete every secondary objective possible.

In addition to this is the Tactical Gear that modifies your armor, giving you your choice of a few squad-affecting special abilities that recharge on a cooldown timer after you use them. Again, you’ll unlock more as you progress, but once I got my hands on the Stim that allowed me to heal myself and any teammates within its radius for a short time, I was never tempted by any of the other choices. All of these customization options evolve the classic Gears of War combat in a welcome but not radical way that I appreciate, while liberally placed Supply Caches let you cycle weapons and mods rather frequently if you so choose.

And you’ll be glad for the ability to rearrange your weapon loadout often in E-Day’s mini-boss fights and full-blown boss battles. Almost all of them are memorable in a good way. With, again, a mix of old and new “faces,” these were often barely-scrape-by bouts during my playthrough and ones I welcomed both when they arrived and when I emerged victorious.

Almost all of the boss fights are memorable in a good way.

E-Day is packed with beautiful locations. The destroyed downtown of Kalona; the pitch-black, Locust-dug caves underneath it; the almost sinister-looking Imulsion refinery; the peaceful mountaintops outside the city. Although the entire campaign doesn’t take place there, you’ll spend a healthy amount of time in Kalona, and the massive but dense battle spaces there are an excellent evolution of the mostly empty open-world areas from Gears 5. The freedom feels far more organic and meaningful here, as there are so many interesting things around almost every corner.

In addition to the aforementioned secondary objectives that grant meaningful Weapon Mod upgrades, there are hidden objects with optionally-viewed details that add a bit of color to a world in the process of recovering from a 79-year civil war, only to be invaded and destroyed by the Locust in a few days. The gorgeous visuals are brought down only by infrequent but noticeable framerate hitches, even while playing in Performance Mode on the Xbox Series X. As such, I can’t recommend playing on the 30fps Quality Mode – at least not before a patch or two.

On a side note, I appreciate that E-Day doesn’t do the all-too-common “make the player run the gauntlet of everything they’ve already fought, but multiply it” endgame sequence. Instead, your mettle is tested plenty of times along the way, with ample quiet moments to punctuate the loud action. And the ending is, I’ll say without spoiling anything, , which isn’t an easy thing to pull off when, as I mentioned, we already know that Marcus and Dom make it out of E-Day alive. And thank goodness, because I need more quippy Marcus Fenix one-liners in my life; I can’t get enough of them.

By going back to the beginning, Gears of War: E-Day returns to the heart of this series: Marcus Fenix, Dom Santiago, and a Locust horde that’s as terrifying as it is dangerous. E-Day pulls off the tightrope act of giving us a heartfelt prequel with strong characters even when we know how it ends. On a more mechanical level, it also evolves the enemies, weapons, and combat you’d expect to deliver a Gears of War campaign that stands toe-to-toe with any of the others. It wraps up with 10 years still left to go before Marcus gets tossed in prison ahead of the events of the first Gears of War, so here’s hoping the next one stays in the past for a while longer – and that we don’t have to wait another seven years for it to arrive.

items.title: East of Eden Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Good vs. evil, brotherly rivalries, parental rejection, the notion of free will as opposed to fate… East of Eden has a lot going on. And the new of the John Steinbeck epic is pretty great at conveying these ideas with a well-acted, handsomely produced, seven-episode miniseries that’s the streaming equivalent of a page-turner.

I confess to having never seen Elia Kazan’s 1955 adaptation of East of Eden in its entirety, despite its status as one of only three starring vehicles for James Dean. But what I do remember about it is mish-mashed in my head with another of his films, Giant, so much so that I was a bit surprised by how the Netflix version ended. That may also be in part because, surprisingly, there haven’t been a ton of film or TV adaptations of East of Eden beyond the Kazan/Dean film; there was a TV miniseries in 1981 starring Jane Seymour, and a long-gestating movie version that had Jennifer Lawrence attached at one point but never materialized, but otherwise that’s it.

And that’s just fine, because now Kazan’s granddaughter, the actress Zoe Kazan, has adapted the 1952 novel for the small screen. Along with directors Garth Davis and Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre, Kazan takes the story and imparts a modern sensibility to what is, after all, an age-old tale. For East of Eden makes no bones about its ultimate source, which is the biblical tale of Cain and Abel. Indeed, the very title comes from the Book of Genesis: “So Cain went out from the presence of the Lord and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.”

Only in this version of the story, the second Black Widow and the third Professor Xavier star! (Also, a former Ghost Rider villain shows up for a supporting turn.) I’m talking, of course, about Florence Pugh, who really is the centerpiece of this version of the story as Cathy Ames, and Christopher Abbott, who is the second lead as Adam Trask. Mike Faist (Challengers) plays Adam’s brother Charles, who winds up in the middle of things between Cathy and Adam even while the latter two are destined to marry and have children someday. East of Eden is a generational story, as we start Episode 1, “Brothers,” in the post-Civil War Connecticut of 1874 and eventually find our way to California’s Salinas Valley circa World War I in the finale, “Timshel.”

Pugh in particular stands out as the complicated, headstrong, smart, and quite evil Cathy.

“I believe there are monsters born in this world to human parents,” Pugh’s Cathy tells us in voiceover in the opening line of the series. And that is certainly an idea that lingers over the 46 years or so of the Trask family that we are to bear witness to, though whereas Cathy – a cruel woman who does unspeakable things to those who love her most – takes that notion to be incontrovertible, Kazan is less convinced. Cathy may be a monster, but was she born that way or did other monsters turn the once innocent child that she was into one of their own?

Episode 1 spends a good amount of time with the young versions of Adam (Costa D'Angelo) and his brother Charles (Tom Sweet), as they are forced to run military drills under their father Cyrus (a hateful Tracy Letts), whose heart is still in the war and who plays favorites with his sons. “Adam, don’t you see? I love you better,” Cyrus tells his elder son while Charles is barely within earshot. And yet he has a funny way of showing this affection, choosing to send Adam off to fight in the army while making Charles – the son who actually has an interest in enlisting – stay home to mind the farm.

By the time Cathy comes into the brothers’ lives years later, she’s on death’s doorstep as well as the Trasks’, having been beaten savagely by forces unknown. She will also soon drive a wedge between Adam and Charles, just as their father did, upending all their lives in the years to come, even while that central question will continue to come up: Are monsters born, or are they made?

East of Eden constantly raises this idea, and sometimes it’s a bit too on the nose about it. “I want to be good” and similar lines are uttered by characters who we already know are struggling with the choices they’ve made, or are about to make. But then it has moments of sublime exploration of such notions. In particular, the relationship that forms between Hoon Lee’s Lee and Ciarán Hinds’ Samuel Hamilton yields a philosophical discussion around the idea of “timshel” – a Hebrew word that, according to Steinbeck’s translation, means “thou mayest.” In other words, you may, or you may not. It’s your choice to do good… or bad.

Hoon Lee (Your Friends & Neighbors) is a standout in this series, eventually entering the picture as the Chinese manservant of Adam’s household who, despite being American born, is still treated as lesser by most of the whites who he lives among. His connection to Adam and Adam’s own sons, and how it leads him to reflect on his own life, is both heartwarming and at times sad. Hinds too plays an important and memorable part in the Trask family as Adam and Cathy move out West, while Joseph Zada and Joe Anders eventually join the series as the years progress, playing twin brothers Caleb and Aron, respectively, and effectively continuing the themes of fraternal friction as 20th century counterparts to their father and uncle.

As for Pugh, Abbott, and Faist, the trio are excellent in their roles, with Pugh in particular standing out as the complicated, headstrong, smart, and quite evil Cathy. Though indeed born of human parents as Cathy was, Zoe Kazan’s East of Eden can’t help but contemplate how even a character like this could be the result of more than just fate. “To a monster, the norm must seem monstrous,” Cathy says in that same voiceover. But what if that monster had no choice but to become monstrous in order to survive?

items.title: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered Review Update
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
As the fantasy RPG GOAT, it really doesn’t take a whole lot for me to replay The Witcher 3. I’ve happily done so the numerous other times developer CD Projekt Red has revamped this masterpiece, but The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered seems to be the biggest overhaul to the beloved tale yet. A free update for anyone who owns the original, so many different parts of this already excellent game have been improved – from combat to movement to skill progression (not to mention the modernized graphics). After about 10 hours working my way through White Orchard and beyond, it’s already extremely clear that this is the best The Witcher 3 has ever been.

Combat is less floaty and enemies are (slightly) less stupid

It’s probably not controversial to say that one of the worst parts of this otherwise amazing adventure was the combat. Even after at least a few updates to it over the years, it still mostly felt floaty, a bit on the sloppy side, and enemies were a huge fan of just standing there and waiting for their turn to get decapitated. The modernizations made to combat in this remaster are its biggest step forward, as a whole bevy of tweaks have been made to address various sticking points. Geralt attacks faster and enemies are quicker to match your pace, which makes the process of chopping through your ninth pack of wolves much less irritating.

The camera and lock-on functionality have been the highlight so far, as you can now toggle between large groups of enemies with ease, and without the camera losing its mind. I didn’t even use the lock-on system in the original specifically because it was so unreliable, so being able to do so now has taken some serious getting used to. In general, the camera feels much better – less tightly locked to your back so you can handle groups of enemies more reliably (though those darn Neckers still like to sneak up on ya), and so far I’ve encountered far fewer situations where I felt like I was fighting my view as much as I was the monsters.

I’ve also noticed some new enemy behaviors that make swordplay more interesting, specifically how they’ll now retreat instead of letting you trounce them with steel, launch less telegraphed counterattacks, and disappear and reappear behind you (in the case of ghost monsters). All that did a much better job of making me feel like I was fighting intelligent creatures. Of course, compared to some of the stuff we see in action games today, I still do feel like the enemy behavior shows its age, and it was never all that great to begin with. Still, this is enough of an improvement to make combat feel much more engaging than it once did, significantly upgrading one of this adventure’s weakest points.

Geralt moves so much faster and Roach is less of a cretin

Movement is one of those small details that can grate the heck out of you in a massive RPG like The Witcher 3, slowly filling you with rage over the course of hundreds of hours. In the original, Geralt was often slow and had a lot of trouble getting over things. His rigid animations sometimes made me avoid ladders altogether because I just didn’t have the patience for it. In the remaster, Geralt absolutely flies over fences and navigates vertical obstacles with relative ease, to the point where it actually felt weird to see him be so nimble. I recall losing over an hour of progress in the 1.0 version when Geralt fell off a ledge no taller than a barstool and managed to break every bone in his body. This was reduced already in the next-gen update from 2022, but combined with the other speed and mobility improvements here, it almost feels like a completely different game – to the point where I’ve begun to wonder if it’ll make the map feel smaller than before as I get deeper in.

Similarly, Roach is no longer the annoying idiot she once was, now sporting much more intuitive controls that make her less likely to get caught on trees (which she now passes through if she’s just brushing against them while galloping), or end up on top of a barn. Most importantly, you can now loot herbs and whatnot without getting off your horse, which is maybe the single best improvement this remaster offers (dismounting every 10 seconds to pick a flower drove me to the brink of madness in 2015).

Skill trees are less restrictive

A pet peeve of mine in RPGs is when skill trees prevent you from playing around with different builds until you get deep into the progression. This is something The Witcher 3 suffered from quite a bit in the early hours, as so many of the impactful abilities were locked behind walls you couldn’t remove until late in the journey. The revised trees in the remaster take a page out of Cyberpunk 2077’s book by making perks more readily available earlier on, so you can customize how you’d like Geralt to get his Witchering done. I’m still early in my journey on this run, but I’m already happy to see that I won’t have to wait until I’ve invested a whole 12 points in a branch before I can unlock any good skills – so long as I’ve purchased a skill along the route I’m focusing on, I can now progress down a certain skill path with fewer obstructions.

Oh, yeah, this remaster looks pretty great too

Maybe this goes without saying for a remaster, but this is a pretty massive graphical upgrade, even over the one The Witcher 3 got for the current generation of consoles just four years ago. The lighting is much more dramatic, environmental textures are way more detailed, shadows and reflections are much more consistent across the board (especially on PC), and Geralt’s hair looks way less like a blurry mess than it once did. Again, this is all stuff that you’d hope would be the bare minimum when remastering a 12-year-old game, but it still warrants a shoutout. There’s even a new photo mode for those of you who want to take glamor shots of Geralt in all his new, high definition glory.

The one thing caveat here is that performance is still not perfect, and I still ran into a dropped frame or two on both console and PC. It’s a small price to pay for how much better things look, though, especially with the incredibly short load times I saw. And considering that the original had some framerate issues of its own, it’s not like anything has gotten here.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered’s greatest asset isn’t that it adds anything the original sorely lacked, but rather that it removes some of the biggest roadblocks to fun the 1.0 version was saddled with. Combat is more challenging but also easier to enjoy, movement is quicker and less irritating, and revised skill trees allow for more freedom. Even if it doesn’t manage to fix some of the technical issues (plus I’m sure there are some bugs waiting for me to encounter them that haven’t reared their ugly heads yet), it manages to make this classic RPG more enjoyable in 2026, and that’s worth yet another ride down its well-trodded roads.

items.title: Beware Boiúna Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Movies about monstrous versions of recognizable animals are a fun subgenre. The likes of Anaconda, Lake Placid, The Meg, and the granddaddy of them all, King Kong, offer a certain innate allure regardless of their differing quality, as they take a creature we might already find menacing and mega-plus-size them. Some lean into camp, some into pure horror, and some into tragedy, but a surprising number of them work on some level.

The latest addition to this type of film is Beware Boiúna, which has its moments and a few clever twists on formulaic situations, but never quite fully takes off. On top of that, the film also suffers from just taking too damn long to get to the giant snake we’re there to see. I want to beware Boiúna, so give me Boiúna!

The film follows a trio of doctors who come to the Amazon on a humanitarian trip to administer medical assistance and, along with the crew of the boat they’re traveling on, run afoul of the legendary Boiúna — a massive fearsome snake from Brazilian mythology who is described almost like a force of nature, dispatching anyone that she sees as upsetting the balance within her home.

Though Beware Boiúna delivers a couple of early death scenes to tease the terrors to come, its set-up is far too prolonged for a film of this sort. Even at 1 hour and 44 minutes, it easily feels 15 minutes too long; Anaconda and Lake Placid knew what they were doing, running 90 minutes or less each. There are ultimately too many scenes establishing the characters and their dynamics, along with an attempt to go for a more serious-minded, grounded feeling than you might expect from a film of this sort. It’s admirable to infuse themes about the exploitation of the Amazon and its indigenous people into a giant snake movie, but it should be done far more efficiently or better blended within the mayhem people are paying to see.

The film also includes a storyline that feels like it’s part of the set-up to a totally different movie, involving a notably dark experience that med student Alli (Jessica Rothe) and ship mechanic Lena (Kiana Madeira) have that leads to “colonizer” Brennan (Logan Marshall-Green) and his men angrily tracking them from a different boat. Sure, it offers up more potential victims for Boiúna, but it’s another place where there was an easier, quicker way to get there.

When Boiúna finally unleashes, she’s pretty cool and very daunting, and the film makes good use of her unreal size as a weapon in its own right… when we can get a good look at her, that is, which isn’t enough. Director Mike P. Nelson and cinematographer Nick Junkersfeld keep Beware Boiúna often looking visually appealing, and the FX used to bring Boiúna are solid in the glimpses we get. But it quickly begins to feel like the film’s low budget is keeping her from being seen nearly as much as one would hope, including resorting to some distracting shaky-cam at points to try to disguise that fact… and this is not nearly a Jaws-level film in terms of making up for its often offscreen beast.

Veteran screenwriter Alan B. McElroy, the writer behind Halloween 4: The Return of Michael Myers — still the best Halloween sequel ever — manages to interject some deviations from the expected formula of this kind of movie. There are solid moments that play with the usual flow of who will die next, whose perspective we’re following, or what character we’re meant to like at any given moment. But at the same time, there’s not enough done in terms of delivering memorable deaths, with too many characters taken out quickly and without discernible details to make their demise stand out.

There’s not enough done in terms of delivering memorable deaths, with too many characters taken out quickly and without discernible details to make their demise stand out. 

And yet there are also well-done scenes involving mosquito eggs left inside a human’s back, a snake smashing into a construction vehicle, or the particular highlight of a character needing to think fast to save themselves using the corpse of a fallen friend. But then that scene is undercut by some unnecessary flashbacks immediately afterward, providing hand-holding we simply don’t need to apparently remind the audience of a relationship we are already fully aware of. Ultimately, there’s just a lot of push-pull here.

Anchoring the film are the likable duo of Rothe and Madeira, projecting the feeling of believable resourcefulness that these characters need to have. It’s too bad Beware Boiúna doesn’t allow for Rothe to show off her impressively strong comedy chops like the Happy Death Day movies do, but better served on that front is Will Close. Close nails each of the funny lines given to his comic relief character of Callum, who’s very much out of his element even before the giant snake arrives.

Director Nelson — recently hired to direct the eleventh Saw movie — shows some flair, including the moments mentioned above or with a couple of well orchestrated jump scares, such as one that cleverly uses blurriness as a set-up. But these “that was cool” beats that are peppered throughout the film never gain enough momentum for the movie to feel like it’s truly locked in. And they can't make up for not having enough Boiúna!

items.title: Scrubs Season 11: Episodes 1 & 2 Review
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
The first two episodes of Scrubs Season 11 premiere on ABC on September 30 and on Hulu on October 1.

In an era where it's become customary to wait years between new seasons of many popular shows, it's certainly a treat to receive two seasons of Scrubs in the same calendar year. The previous revival season proved to be the ultimate sitcom comfort food. It effortlessly wiped away the stigma of Season 9 and won fans back over with its depiction of the eternal bromance between Drs. John Dorian (Zach Braff) and Christopher Turk (Donald Faison). Season 10 wasn't without its problems, but it was a fun little romp that recaptured the charming vibe of the original series. Season 11 is much the same, but with a slightly more ambitious storytelling approach added for good measure.

Naturally, Braff and Faison remain in the spotlight for Season 11, as does Sarah Chalke's Dr. Elliot Reid. Much of the new cast introduced in Season 10 also returns, with Ava Bunn's Sam Tosh now upped to series regular. Unfortunately, Season 11 eliminates two of the more memorable supporting cast members in Joel Kim Booster's Dr. Kevin Park and X Mayo's Nurse Pippa Raymond. It's not the worst thing in the world for the series to trim its ensemble cast a bit, but neither character deserved to be on the chopping block.

Season 10 did suffer at times from the lack of focus on classic Scrubs characters like Dr. Cox (John C. McGinley) and Nurse Carla Espinosa (Judy Reyes). Thankfully, that changed late in the game as the now-retired Dr. Cox came roaring back into Sacred Heart and grappled with his own mortality. One of the perks of Season 11 is that it continues that storyline rather than simply moving on. In fact, there are hints of a more serialized narrative this season. The show really leans into Cox's ongoing health struggles and J.D.'s desperate attempts to care for his prickly mentor.
