Mind you, Scrubs is in no danger of turning into The Pitt anytime soon, but it is nice to get a bit more drama and see a little more connective tissue between these first two episodes. And if that approach keeps McGinley's hilarious character in the picture longer this season, so much the better.

If Scrubs is being a bit more ambitious with its storytelling this season, it certainly never loses sight of the fact that fans are here first and foremost for the dynamic between J.D., Turk, and Elliot. All three characters get ample room to shine in these first two episodes. J.D and Turk have several memorable bonding scenes together, and the series is ever on-point with J.D.'s fanciful dream sequences. There's one cutaway that rivals Season 10's detective noir scene for its sheer zaniness. And with Elliot, the series continues finding ways to explore and enrich the character outside the shackles of the "Will they, won't they?" format the original series was so fixated on.

But what of the newbies? As enjoyable as it was, Season 10 never fully cemented its new cast of interns. There were simply too many of these characters, and they never felt like a priority for the series amid the emphasis on the core doctor trinity. These two episodes show signs that the writers are looking to narrow their focus a bit this time. Obviously, Bunn's Tosh is a bigger priority now, and Episode 2 makes some inroads in terms of defining her as more than "the social media-obsessed one."

In fact, Episode 2, which is titled "My Mentee," seems to cement a new status quo where each of the three leads is paired with a different underling, mirroring the Cox/J.D. dynamic of the original show. Elliott gets Tosh, Turk gets Dr. Dashana Trainor (Amanda Morrow), and J.D. struggles to connect with the new chief resident, Dr. Grant Summers (John Higgins). This narrowed focus is promising, though it does serve to make the rest of the interns like Asher (Jacob Dudman) and Blake (David Gridley) feel even more superfluous than before. We'll see if Season 11 can ultimately achieve a better balance than its predecessor, but things are looking promising so far.

items.title: End of Abyss Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
The satisfaction of the metroidvania genre comes from a sensation of mastery – taking a place I'm unfamiliar with and slowly unraveling its complexities until I command dominance over its spaces and the threats that perpetually lurk within. For its debut game, End of Abyss, developer Section 9 Interactive tries to apply that format to an atmospheric horror adventure with twin-stick controls and instills a striking sense of dread inside a gargantuan labyrinthian facility. Its atmosphere only carries it so far, though; End of Abyss's exploration and combat slowly descend into a slog, and it never fully recovers from feeling like a routine procedure.

End of Abyss is centered around a young combat technician named Cel, who isn't given much in the way of personality. Cel is a silent observer who's trained to interact with the world through the scope of a gun. They skulk around this massive, desolate complex with only a few other soldiers four times their size, slowly attempting to discern what happened here. The place is abandoned, seemingly run by a series of AI boxes known as Security Control Units, which are trying to keep the facility from falling into total disarray. A mysterious voice calls out to Cel through these boxes, hoping they will help free this place from the zombified station workers who turned into enemy Husks.

Without much else explained, Cel is thrust into the cold concrete corridors and expected to survive. As I walked through dimly lit hallways and parasitic flea-infested tunnels, it was clear Section 9 was built of former Little Nightmares developers. The clay-doll aesthetic and isometric perspective is immediately recognizable. Atmosphere is the most captivating thing End of Abyss has to offer.

The grotesque detritus of vacant bedrooms litters the Habitation Sector, crafting a harrowing and bone-chilling opening section. I walked through every doorway with my thumb trembling on the right stick. Even with Cel's pistol drawn to keep my guard up, I was still terrified of what could be on the other side. The way a light flickers above an exit or how an enemy body encased in parasitic fungus is positioned all constantly feed into the uneasiness you want from a horror experience. These tricks work for the first few hours, but as End of Abyss dragged on, I began to see the seams of it all, and it eventually became too familiar.

What were once terrifying jump scares became predictable.

What were once terrifying jump scares became predictable – corpses with important items conveniently placed in large open arenas consistently led to combat encounters I knew were coming. The supposedly dead enemies I used to fear waking up to chase me down always would, and thus it became routine to start shooting them before I even approached.

The mystery surrounding End of Abyss unsatisfyingly relied on the absence of information. Characters trade in vague uncertainties, often offering up little to no useful information about how or why we are in this facility. A few notes and documents are found scattered around its hallowed halls, but even slowly learning about what life was like here before our protagonist Cel touched down does little to actually paint a compelling picture. I pushed forward, turning on little AI boxes around this compound to activate an elevator, I searched for power cells to switch on a beacon, and I eventually descended into the dreaded lower levels to see what lurked below.

It wasn't until the back third of End of Abyss’ roughly 10-hour campaign that the plot started to gain momentum. The story suddenly took a front seat as characters began to explain the reason for our deadly trek through the compound. But because the buildup lacked tangible stakes, it was mystery for mystery's sake, and rarely did it feel of any consequence.

That's not to say that End of Abyss doesn't have its moments. Particularly in the last act when tiptoeing around the lower levels, I found note after note that brought me closer into the horrors of this world. Rooms filled with strange new oddities and remnants of experimentations piqued my curiosity and illustrated an underlying terror.

A few new weapons to add to my parasite killing arsenal also kept me invested in the search-action. Your options range from the Pulse Gun, a trusty and reliable pistol with unlimited ammo, to a flamethrower that lights up entire rooms in a wall of fire. The twin-stick shooter part of End of Abyss is no joke, either. Combat encounters can swing drastically if you roll the wrong way or get caught in a corner. I always felt in control of the situation even as I dipped and dodged through large hordes of enemies. So when I would slip up and lose that control, it became a struggle to regain my footing. That's where the combat thrives: walking on the razor's edge between confidence and hubris with a little uncertainty.

Enemy variety pushed me to do some experimentation in the action. Grenades were a staple in large group encounters, learning to manipulate aggressive enemy behavior to my advantage became a small game on its own, and grouping up mobs to maximize a red barrel explosion was a key tactic. More challenging enemies, like the long-necked Husk Latcher, made keeping a safe distance difficult; it perpetually charged forward and swung its long-reaching, claw-like head in my direction.

While I found the moment-to-moment combat mostly strong, the boss fights feel rote by comparison. Circular arenas with large creatures played out largely the same – roll away from the boss, pop a few shots into them, rinse and repeat. Some bosses, like the Centipede Husk, mixed things up a bit by leaving the arena and popping out of different corners to try and catch me off guard. Other fights are more focused on dumping large amounts of ammunition into the boss, and that's disappointing for a game with flashes of brilliance.

With the exception of the pistol, you'll need to manage your ammo and craft more at workbenches found around the different save points throughout the facility. Early on, managing my Riot Breaker shotgun ammo and choosing to save my limited supply for the moments that mattered felt reminiscent of other survival horror games like Resident Evil. However, after only a couple of hours, I rarely thought about my ammo counts, since the materials required to craft more bullets at a workbench felt like drops in a bucket. This trend continued as I acquired the Security Rifle – an armor-piercing long-range gun – and that minimized a potentially interesting dynamic.

Fragments are found around every corner, and they're a plentiful currency throughout. I found them on dead enemies, stashed away in lockers and treasure chests, and just laying in optional rooms. It was so abundant that I eventually felt nothing every time I saw that blue glow in the distance.

This resource problem began to seep into the cracks of the foundation and expose a larger problem: exploration is not truly rewarding. The interconnected hallways and twisting systems that make understanding how all of the locations fit together are part of the puzzle in a metroidvania. But here, the further I dove into the depths of it all, the more frustrating navigating this dilapidated station became. The lack of visual variety and identity across different areas made everything look the same, and it was difficult to pinpoint points of interest in an area to help anchor myself. End of Abyss became more about looking at the map every few seconds to ensure I wasn't going the wrong way than soaking in the foreboding atmosphere that surrounded me.

Unlocking shortcuts with keycards or opening a door from the opposite side didn't bring revelation or satisfaction. It often brought confusion about how or why these rooms were tied together and what use this shortcut would have. When every zone is the same gray-and-blue hue, it becomes a tired cycle to open up another cold steel door for the sake of it, or for a handful of Fragments I didn't really need. For every new weapon or piece of equipment I found, there were five rooms full of just Fragments.

And then there was the Containment Sector. This section of the map leaks radiation and would slowly tick away at my health if I stayed in the area. I quickly shifted gears and locked in, moving with surgical precision as I couldn't waste any time getting lost. Every few minutes my health would tick to zero, I would die, and I would respawn at a nearby checkpoint. It felt obvious that there was something I was missing, some sort of protection from the radiation, since the further into the sector I went, the stronger the radiation became.

To its credit, the tone-setting audio design is some of the best I've heard recently.

Eventually I discovered a radiation suit mod that protected me from the constant damage. Instead of elation, all I felt was relief that I was done having to poke and prod random corners of this world for something that may or may not have existed. This entire scavenger hunt felt so detached from the Containment Sector and what I was trying to accomplish there, and it's a disconnect that even metroidvanias of yore didn't have.

Backtracking in End of Abyss is rough, even with a transit system that can take you to most zones. Cel does not move very quickly while sprinting, and the constant aimless roaming really pads out the overall runtime. These problems are exacerbated by multiple bugs that prevented me from progressing – random invisible walls that would stop me dead in my tracks on a ladder or prevent me from doubling back to a section I was just in. This caused me to have to restart at a previous checkpoint, losing 10-15 minutes of progress each time.

Despite the frustrations with exploration, the tone-setting audio design from Section 9 is some of the best I've heard recently. Pulsating reverberations of loud clangs and distorted gurgles rang through my headphones, sending shivers down my spine. The wet squelching of enemies as they scurried toward me made me want to crawl out of my skin. The audio gives End of Abyss a sense of scope that outsized its dark and tight corridors, making it feel like this facility goes far beyond the bounds of the screen.

items.title: Slow Horses Season 6, Episode 3 Review — ‘Resurrection’
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
This review contains full spoilers for Season 6, Episode 3, which is streaming on Apple TV now.

For as apt a title as “Resurrection” is for this particular Slow Horses episode, it also kind of undersells the amount of resurrecting — literal and otherwise — within. It’s a trifecta: Of course, there’s Sid (Olivia Cooke), who was revealed to be alive at the end of the last episode. But then there’s Louisa Guy (Rosalind Eleazar), living a new plush life in the corporate world whose past life as a Slow Horse is unmercifully revived when Shirley Dander (Aimee-Ffion Edwards) and Catherine Standish (Saskia Reeves) drag her out of a meeting. Lastly, there’s Moira (Joanna Scanlan), who might have actually been dead for a minute or two after the hit attempt by the murder twins (Kyle Soller and MyAnna Buring), springing back to life. “Resurrection” is a real doozy and an overall excellent Slow Horses episode that takes full advantage of all the plot-building groundwork this season has done thus far.

It kicks off with River’s (Jack Lowden) understandably bemused expression watching Sid prance around his grandfather’s kitchen as if almost nothing had happened. He asks all the same questions we as viewers have: How? Why? What the hell, man? But their conversation is cut short as the murderers — who apparently have names (rather, obvious aliases), Jim and Jane — pull up on the long driveway to cross off their next hit. It starts an episode-long cat-and-mouse game between the two pairs that makes space for fun banter (ie., how much a cow costs) and big developments to the grander season conspiracy (the murderers are Russian, some of Sid’s current story).

It’s a thrilling framework that also reminds us of both the bumbling and occasionally competent sides of a Slow Horse. When Jim and Jane first break into the house after a lame attempt at non-forced entry (“We’re lost” — try harder!), I braced myself: Will River and Sid do some cool spy shit and take them out? The thought was answered with a cut to them sprinting through the field to escape. Again and again, they find a moment to breathe and unpack the lost years until Jim and Jane have found the end of the scent trail that leads directly back to Sid and River. The very end of the episode is no different: Just when you think the Slow Horses have shaken their tail, Jim and Jane come ominously skulking through the parking lot. (Coe, do something!)

Of course, “Resurrection” isn’t just the River and Sid show. The women of Slough House have formed a ragtag little band with Louisa and Moira in tow to keep in line with Blake’s grave protocol. Louisa is a welcome familiar face and the lingering effects of Moira’s gas poisoning give her some funny moments of delirium, but this team-up keeps up the weakest part of the season thus far: Standish continuing to grieve her ex-boss Charles Partner while suppressing her urge to drink. It’s a real shame that she's been mostly sidelined to staring at wine racks so far given that she’s so often been an integral supporting role in the series.

Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas), however, has been given plenty to do — such is the life of First Desk — and is Going Through It after her disastrous interview with Talkpoint. Pretty much everyone has a bone to pick with her right now, and she takes it out on Emma Flyte (Ruth Bradley), demoting her from her head Dog duties and banishing her to Slough House. I can’t help but wonder how much more of this pressure Diana can take before her deflective front starts to erode. Or maybe she really is an impenetrable force after all!

Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman) and Roddy Ho (Christopher Chung) have their own side quest, too, in picking up Reece Nesmith (Lenny Rush), the son of the ex-Dog that Frank Harkness (Hugo Weaving) strangled last episode — and sole witness to his murder. Given that Lamb is actually good at his job, they find Reece, who proves to be quite the match for both of his captors (and can go fart-to-fart against Lamb). Unfortunately for Reece, decades of experience beats out the energy of youth.

items.title: Digger Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
opens in theaters on October 2.

"Gentlemen, we find ourselves in a dildo of a pickle," says the President of the United States as he comes to grips with the fact that a US oil-drilling mishap has split off a city-sized ice shelf that's on a path of destruction toward Europe and will trigger tsunamis, causing untold death and destruction. That line, exquisitely delivered by John Goodman and imposingly photographed by director Alejandro G. Iñárritu (Babel, Birdman, The Revenant) in his signature low, wide-angle style, also sums up my complex feelings toward a film whose reach far exceeds its grasp and whose satire—while funny—would have felt fresher a decade ago.

Starting with an ice fracture "10 times the size of his own dick," Digger follows Digger Rockwell, the oil tycoon responsible for the ice shelf debacle mentioned above, who finds himself on the defensive as he works with the president, advisors and generals to try to stop the impending doom brought on by our insatiable appetite for fossil fuels—and when that fails, at the very least, to "control the narrative."

There's a twist that the marketing seems to be deliberately trying to avoid, so I won't directly mention it in this review. However, it fundamentally affects my opinion of the film. I'll talk around it and also fence it in with "Possible Spoiler" warnings.

But let's get right to the best part of the show: Tom Cruise.

It's been a long time since Tom Cruise has taken on a role that required zero action. I was excited for him to enter his post-Mission: Impossible era and was delighted to see elements of Digger Rockwell echo Tropic Thunder's Les Grossman.

For Digger Rockwell, Cruise dons heavy prosthetics to fully transform into the wily old oil tycoon. His look may be more Ross Perot, but it’s still clear an action star is under all that latex, climbing mantles and dancing with his shovel. Whether he's bickering with Riz Ahmed about his annoying scientific ethics or lecturing world leaders on why he's necessary—the latter of which is one of the best scenes in the film and might be worth the price of admission alone—Cruise's performance is both focused and kinetic.

Digger lecturing a United Nations-type body is Cruise's "you can't handle the truth!" monologue and might be one of the best of his career. His "You demand. I supply" rhetoric echoes Colonel Jessup's "[you] sleep under the blanket of the very freedom I provide, and then you question the manner in which I provide it" speech. Instead of Nicholson's fierce but measured delivery (which Nerdwriter expertly broke down in his Jack Nicholson: The Art of Anger video essay), Digger delivers this whole speech while pacing the set and even physically fighting with some listeners in one unbroken take.

For every Tom Cruise action movie, there's some featurette of the filmmakers marveling at his ability to deliver a line while he's dangling from a building or strapped to the side of a plane. Digger's monologue, where he conjures up an almost 1,000-word lecture without cutting, all while hitting the constantly moving camera blocking, is as stunning an accomplishment and as mesmerizing as any of those action scenes.

This scene isn't just Tom at his best; it's also Iñárritu and longtime collaborator, cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki, upping their game too. This Digger oner combines the complex blocking of background and extras from Birdman's Times Square underwear jaunt with the more dialogue-heavy long shots Iñárritu and Lubezki experimented with in The Revenant to create a stunning one-shot that showcases Cruise's acting chops in a way we haven't seen in decades, if ever.

Digger's monologue is as stunning an accomplishment and as mesmerizing as any of Tom Cruise's past action scenes.

Thematically, this monologue is one of the few times the satire actually says something pointed. Most of the film relies on a Looney Tunes-esque, Yosemite Sam diplomacy: We need oil at any cost and American weapons and brute force can solve any problem nature presents.

Digger's speech provides a smart contrast to the President's mean-spirited, selfish, extremely aggressive, and idiotic decisions. His monologue deftly navigates a complex and evolving argument that starts with that "You demand, I supply" line before chastising the attendees for profiting royally from his companies, explaining that the masses are too poor to care, and finally lecturing them that they've inadvertently chosen his side in these matters, so they better pray he wins.

Digger represents the status quo, personified. Iñárritu uses this monologue as the film's sharpest argument for how Digger and company's poor decision-making got them into an environmental catastrophe that these fossil fools are too ill-equipped to solve.

This is a film about how methane leaks caused by the prolonged burning of fossil fuels, combined with an oil-drilling fiasco, created an environmental catastrophe that the film's clearly conservative leadership is ill-equipped to deal with. To avoid bringing politics into this review is a diplomatic exercise that only John Goodman's president would be stupid enough to pursue.

Political satire doesn't need to be subtle, but it does need to illuminate something beyond the obvious by pushing story elements like recognizable characters, plots, and events to their logical extremes. Unfortunately, the script by Iñárritu, Alexander Dinelaris, Nicolás Giacobone, and Sabina Berman fails to provoke any profound truth or unique thinking. The end of this global-warming disaster satire lands exactly where you think it will. Regrettably for Digger, there are other films like Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up that have tackled the same topics, but in more interesting ways.

There’s been a lot of reporting on the mixed early impressions of Digger. Don't Look Up’s reaction was also mixed. It currently has a 56% on Rotten Tomatoes. But 7/10, and I more or less agree with our review. McKay's different, and in my opinion, smarter approach to the topic—using an asteroid impact as a metaphor for global warming—created a more nuanced take on the subject. He used an objectively obvious catastrophe to contrast our society's inability to do anything to stop it because of our culture's unholy mix of greed, politics, and misinformation.

Digger does the exact opposite of Don't Look Up: Instead of indecision, things go worse because the film's leaders make profoundly stupid decisions. Digger still made me laugh at a decent amount of the jokes, but the film will probably alienate a large part of the audience due to the cartoonishly selfish and negligent conservative politicians and businessmen—characters like Goodman's President Compson and his cabinet, who embody the most negative stereotypes of the American right wing. Meanwhile, some on the other side might bristle at rampant machismo and misogyny that are done in the name of satire.

"Controlling the Narrative"

There's a twist in Digger. I'm going to talk around it here.

A big theme in Digger is "controlling the narrative," which Digger believes is crucial to maintaining power. To that end, we need to talk about Jesse Plemons' character.

I've lamented how unrefined the film's characters are. Only twice does its blunt satire say something interesting: the first is Digger's monologue, and the second is a speech from Plemons' character.

When I left the theater, it was Plemons' monologue that kept me thinking about the film. Without getting too deep into spoilers, his monologue touches on themes explored in the 2022 documentary All the Beauty and the Bloodshed, a film about how the Sackler family used its money to fund the arts to rehabilitate its image after its role in America's opioid crisis. Plemons' character smartly touches on these same ideas, putting an interesting spin on Digger's story in the final act.

End of possible spoilers.

There's A Lot of Great Work on Display

There's an old filmmaking adage: "You can make a bad movie from a good script, but you can't make a good movie from a bad script." Unfortunately, the script is Digger's Achilles heel. But that doesn't mean there isn't some exceptional work on display.

From frame one, it's completely obvious that this movie looks expensive. From evocative murals to stylized miniature work to window vistas that look like amazing natural history museum dioramas, production designer Dennis Gassner created a world that is overflowing with detail and style worthy of a Wes Anderson movie.

Riz Ahmed, who plays Ganesh, Digger's lead scientist and the voice of reason, spars frequently with Tom Cruise, making for some of the film's best exchanges. This probably won't be the movie that lands Cruise his acting statue, but Ahmed turns in the kind of generous supporting performance that Cruise was known for in the late '80s and early '90s which helped his co-stars land Academy Awards.

John Goodman also delivers a stellar performance as President Compson. He has some of the best lines, and you can tell he had a hell of a time delivering them on set.

items.title: The Simpsons Season 38 Premiere Review: 'The Children's Book Job'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for

Nothing is certain in life but death, taxes, and new seasons of The Simpsons. It's pretty incredible to think that this iconic animated sitcom has crossed the 800-episode mark and is now entering its 38th season. That said, the series doesn't do anything particularly noteworthy to ring in the new season. "The Children's Book Job" settles for delivering a fairly standard late-era Simpsons adventure, one that's mostly carried on the back of its guest star.

The conflict this week comes as Marge (Julie Kavner) is no sooner sworn in as PTA president than the town learns Springfield Elementary is about to be shut down. That in itself seems like a decent premise for a new episode. How do you save this beloved Springfield institution? Should the town even want to, given how legendarily terrible Springfield Elementary is?

But that's not the direction writer Dan Vebber opts to go with this particular storyline. Instead, Marge and her fellow parents put all their eggs in the basket of beloved children's book author Constance Clavinger (Emma Thompson). Apparently, having Constance read her latest creation in public is the key to keeping Springfield Elementary's doors open? I wish I knew that when my local district was deciding to shut down my daughter's school...

It's a slightly weird and random pivot, but whatever. As mentioned before, it's really all about this week's celebrity guest voice. Thompson is a real hoot as Constance, an eccentric personality who's both charmingly British and enough of a drunken mess to give Homer (Dan Castellaneta) a run for his money. We also get a brief cameo from Colin Jost, but this is really Thompson's show to steal at the end of the day. She brings her A-game, making the most of her character's many wild mood swings and even belting out a tune with Castellaneta for good measure.

Plot-wise, "The Children's Book Job" is nothing special. This episode is yet another opportunity for Homer to prove he can be reliable and dependable and isn't fully checked out of the fatherhood game. I do appreciate that it doesn't take the cynical route, but instead focuses on Homer earnestly trying to manage Constance's nonstop brand of mischief. The ending is also sweet, as Homer manages to pierce through Constance's jaded heart and convince her not to sabotage her life's work. But still, this is nothing we haven't seen 1000 times before on the Homer/Marge front.

There are a few other noteworthy moments worth calling out in the premiere. It makes solid use of the wider Springfield supporting cast, whether it's Moe (Hank Azaria) calling for a Squid Game-style bloodbath or Snake (Azaria) briefly allying himself with Homer's cause. It would be pretty funny if the series actually followed up on that plot thread and the destruction of Homer's beloved car, but somehow, I doubt that'll happen. I also got a kick out of Marge's passive-agressive responses to Lisa's (Yeardley Smith) various helpful suggestions.

But if there's anything in this episode that stands out as much as Thompson's character, it's the brief chase sequence where Homer hallucinates a journey through various children's books. It's a well-animated bit with fun nods to everything from classics like Madeleine and Richard Scarry to modern fare like Captain Underpants. That's one way to spice up an otherwise textbook Homer storyline.

items.title: Minecraft Dungeons 2 Review
items.author: jon Burgess
items.content:
One of the reasons Minecraft is my favorite game of all time is how alluring its world of endless possibilities is, so it’s a little strange that the Minecraft Dungeons series seems to represent the exact opposite. Minecraft Dungeons 2 is a brief, forgettable ARPG that’s as thin as they come, from its barebones story to its shallow gameplay, and you can see almost all it has to offer in the span of an afternoon. Simple, easygoing action is kinda the whole point here, but while there’s nothing actively offensive about this humdrum adventure, there’s also very little worth getting excited about either. The good news is that the minor improvements this sequel makes over the original are quite welcome, including more customizable characters and the added ability to jump, plus the new realm of the Sift adds some fresh color and creatures to the Minecraft universe – so if you’re looking to spend a mindless night or two swinging swords with your friends, you could do a lot worse than this.

If you didn’t play the first one, Minecraft Dungeons 2 takes the pixelated items and goofy mobs from Minecraft and throws them into an extremely light (and noticeably less gory) version of Diablo. You’ll delve into dungeons, smack around swarms of monsters, and tackle big ol’ slobbery bosses while hoovering up as much loot as you can along the way. But where most ARPGs lean hard into dizzying skill trees and loot with so many different stats you need a degree in mathematics to comprehend them, Minecraft Dungeons strips away most of that in favor of a much simpler framework. That makes it both more approachable and, almost equally, less interesting. While this sequel expands on the ideas from the first in modest ways, like by increasing the armor slots you’ve got from one to four, it mostly maintains that stripped down buildcrafting philosophy.

The roughly seven-hour story has your unnamed hero squaring off against an evil cabal of Illagers who gain access to a new dimension, called the Sift, and… actually, look at that, I’ve just about covered it all. The cutscenes and conversations to be found here are basically just a vague outline of a story that sends you to and fro to kill things and save the world, and that’s about as deep as it ever gets. It’s not like I was expecting some kind of emotional drama from my “Minecraft meets Diablo” game, but like most things in this adventure, there’s still very little to it.

The action is thankfully more developed than the story, adding some key features to the mix that make battling through the blocky world more enjoyable. I had completely forgotten, for example, that the original didn’t have a jump button, and having one here adds some needed platforming and light puzzles to solve – plus it gives you access to a new jump attack so you can drop a ‘bow on these filthy adds. You also have more options for enchanting your weapons and armor with special effects (which you unlock by conquering dungeons and completing quests throughout the world) as well as new artifacts that offer passive buffs, like increased damage with ranged weapons. All of these things are a decent step up from the original, but the vast majority of the moment-to-moment gameplay remains largely unchanged, and smacking samey zombies and Illagers tends to run thin quite quickly.

How your build feels is largely at the mercy of the RNG gods.

The fact that buildcrafting is mostly left up to whichever odd equipment you happen to stumble upon, rather than a class-based system, also means you and your co-op teammates all play exactly the same way, and you rarely have control over how your build feels (at least until you near the endgame), since you’re largely at the mercy of the RNG gods. For example, I wanted to play a rogue-type class, but kept finding big ass swords and tank-like items, so I ended up serving as our crew’s defacto melee fighter despite my best efforts. Not that there’s much of a difference anyway, since every player has access to the exact same dodge skill, base speed, weapon options, etc. and you won’t find a shield to add blocking to your arsenal or anything like that.

The handful of equipment slots you’re given offer a few perks each, like increased DPS or added benefits from using healing items, or the ability to shoot fireworks that explode and deal damage to everything in the vicinity (which are good for ringing in the new year, too). You’ll also find a small arsenal of melee and ranged weapons with which to thwack creepers and skeletons, each with just a single attack pattern for you to spam. As you progress, you’ll be able to add some neat enchantments to give weapons and armor a new perk, like one that makes you move faster after you score a kill, or another that lets your ranged attacks penetrate through a target, but none of them do much to shake up the hollow hacking and slashing.

The best part of Minecraft Dungeons 2 is the new area called the Sift, a magical, soul-powered realm filled with goat things, poisonous water, and more teal landscapes than was previously thought possible with the science of our day. This isn’t a game with a whole lot of personality, and it often feels like it merely wears a thin Minecraft skin – but this new dimension is one of the few ways in which it branches out to do its own thing, and it mostly succeeds at being an interesting place to explore. It’s got some new creatures and a super distinct vibe, with souls floating everywhere and dancing automatons roaming about. Unfortunately, this isn’t the best showcase of the new realm, since you’re mostly just plowing through areas killing things, so it really just made me wish I could wander around it in regular Minecraft. But in a game with not a whole lot of exciting stuff going on, getting to explore this new slice of the Minecraft universe was definitely a highlight.

Once you’ve completed the story, you’ll unlock the equally thin endgame, which adds a new activity called Soul Storms. These events summon more deadly enemies for a chance at better loot, but there aren’t really any other activities to pursue where you’ll really need this better gear – at least not yet. Mojang has said it has plans to roll out additional endgame content after launch, which could make this activity worth grinding some day, but for now it feels mostly like more of the same monotonous chopping and dodging I’d already had enough of by the end of the story. The new equipment, which adds an additional perk to all the weapons and armor you find within this elite tier, is a decent prize at least, so even though I immediately felt like there wasn’t much for me to do with my new kit, there’s something about obtaining cool stuff that’s a worthy end in itself.

Beyond the Soul Storms, you’ll mostly roam around, complete any side quests you hadn’t gotten to yet, replay boss fights from the story, and conquer the numerous optional dungeons that can unlock some new enchantment options for your gear. That’s all fine, but it’s all the same button mashing that will have worn out its welcome by that point. My friends and I tried to find reasons to stick around, curious if the story was just a primer for a more deep, compelling endgame (as is often the case with ARPGs), but it seems like that just hasn’t been built yet.

items.title: Get Jiro Series Premiere Review: Anthony Bourdain's Graphic Novel Comes to Adult Swim
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
This is a spoiler-free review of the first episode of Get Jiro, which premieres on Adult Swim on October 3 and HBO Max on October 4.

It's been close to a decade since Anthony Bourdain's passing, and the sting hasn't faded. Bourdain was such an interesting personality who brought a unique perspective to the worlds of food and travel. It only stands to reason that perspective would also translate to fiction writing. The graphic novel Get Jiro has now been adapted into an animated series on Adult Swim, and the series is well worth a watch for anyone who considers themselves a Bourdain fan.

Based on the graphic novels co-written by Bourdain and Joel Rose and illustrated by Langdon Foss and Alé Garza, Get Jiro is set in a vaguely post-apocalyptic version of Los Angeles where society has all but collapsed and chefs are now the true power players. The idea being that, as humanity turns inward and becomes ever more obsessed with virtual reality and online entertainment, food is now the only pleasure that can't be digitized. Amid this new world order, a humble sushi chef named Jiro (Brian Tee) embarks on a quest for vengeance.

Basically, Get Jiro takes the tropes of a straightforward revenge thriller and embellishes the whole package by submerging it in the culinary arena. What might have been an overly formulaic story were it to star mobsters and assassins becomes something far more weird and compelling when knife-wielding chefs instead take center stage. This world is strange, surreal, and more than a little cut from the Blade Runner cloth, and it works. It's a satire that doesn't feel too out of line with our actual reality.

The titular character anchors the first episode well. Tee's Jiro is extremely soft-spoken and taciturn, but we learn everything we need to through his actions and his behavior around his fellow chefs and food suppliers. He's a character whose talent for creating mouth-watering delicacies is matched only by his skill with a blade. Again, he's a character who might come across as a little too generic in a more traditional crime thriller/martial arts setting, but the food angle helps keep things fresh and exciting.

In fact, Get Jiro's first episode is often at its best when it simply lingers on the act of making food. There's a Miyazaki-esque emphasis on the rote tasks and silent motions that go into cooking. The show's animation style is solid in general (if a bit stiff in motion), but those quieter scenes are where it shines the most, and where Bourdain's own influence is most evident.

The pilot is also adept at introducing the show's other key players, including rival mafioso chefs voiced by Titus Welliver and Alison Pill. These antagonist characters are perhaps a bit too broadly rendered for their own good, but once again, the food angle does help to offset that a bit. And with the graphic novel being given a full 10-episode adaptation, there's ample room to flesh out these characetrs as Jiro's bloody quest unfolds.

items.title: Lanterns Season 1, Episode 7 Review & Recap: 'The Jordan Boys Legacy'
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Lanterns Season 1, Episode 7!

The worst part about Lanterns finally diving into the 2026 storyline first teased back in the pilot is that it forces us into a post-Hal Jordan reality. So much of the appeal of the series rests on the sour dynamic between Kyle Chandler's Hal and Aaron Pierre's John Stewart, and there's just something missing without the former in play. Thankfully, there's a workaround in the form of the Halogram backup. Episode 7 exploits that loophole for all its worth, resulting in a new installment that digs far deeper into Hal's troubled psyche and dark family legacy.

Fittingly, this week kicks off with a flashback to Hal's childhood, where we finally meet Martin Jordan (Jake B. Miller) in the flesh. That opening sequence offers some valuable insight into Hal's character. We can see how Martin casually fostered the same sort of fearlessness in his son that the Stewarts mercilessly drilled into John. And we also get a taste of the deep-seated, suicidal depression that is clearly a generational legacy in Hal's family. Miller really shines in his brief time in the spotlight, expertly conveying Martin's bravado and pain in equal measure. And I have to assume the Sinestro-esque mustache is intentional, a subtle reminder of how much the orphaned Hal would come to look to his GL mentor as a father figure.

From there, things shift back to 2026, as the Halogram reacts to being dug up and reactivated after another 10-year hiatus. Again, the series makes the most of its ability to work around Hal's murder. We get that all-important Hal/John banter back, but with the twist that comes from having a slightly younger and less mean-spirited version of Hal in the mix. It's endlessly entertaining to watch the two interact and for the Halogram to convey some of the things his flesh-and-blood self could never admit.

We're also treated to a terrific scene involving Sheriff Kerry (Kelly Macdonald) reuniting with "Hal," one that features arguably Macdonald's strongest performance in the series to date. I'm not prepared to discount the theory that she was Hal's killer just yet (particularly if it somehow involved her protecting her son), but her grief is clearly genuine regardless.

"The Jordan Boys Legacy" does share one flaw with Episode 6. The drama involving the other Rushville locals just isn't that compelling. Granted, this episode doesn't suffer nearly as much in that regard because it's so much more focused on Hal and John's investigation, but there are still a few scenes focused on these less compelling subplots. I really can't bring myself to care about the blackmail conflict between John and Maggie (Hannah Christine Shetler). So he's out $315,000 and a fancy Richard Mille watch. Why does any of that matter in the grander scheme of John's Green Lantern origin story?

It's also tough to know what to make of the Noah (Shea Pritchard) of it all. On the surface, his little Hat Day runaround isn't that compelling, either. But there's obviously something deeper at work with the character. I fully suspect we'll learn in the finale that he's some sort of human/Manhunter hybrid and is at the heart of Hal's murder (assuming Hal is even dead, which we really can't). I'm just glad the series is running out of room to prolong that particular mystery.

Finally, Episode 7 ends with John stepping foot onto an alien world for the first time. We quickly discover that Hal bequeathed a portal to Antaan's (Paul Ben-Victor) home planet, offering a glimpse of the devastation Manhunters can wreak. It's a nice change of pace seeing a setting other than Earth, even if the flat, featureless desert doesn't make for the most memorable view. It's more Stephanie Economou's eerie, discordant score that makes this setting feel hostile and otherwordly.

After a tense fear gas sequence and some more heart-to-heart moments between Hal and John, we're treated to a proper payoff to the entire sequence with the long-overdue return of Ulrich Thomsen's Sinestro. Naturally, him being marooned on a dead world instead of locked away on Oa raises more questions than it answers, but it's enough simply to see the character again. I just hope Episode 8 has enough room to address these many lingering questions and still wrap up John's season-long arc in a satisfying way. There's still a lot of ground left to cover.

items.title: Godzilla Minus Zero Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
This review is based on a screening timed to the New York Film Festival. opens in theaters in Japan on November 3 and in North America on November 6.

Godzilla movies have long had a problem: What do you do after the initial thrill of a quote/unquote Godzilla origin story? Can the filmmakers somehow continue the deep thematic underpinnings of that first adventure, even while upping the visual ante with more giant monster action? How do you offer a probing commentary about the world we live in – which is what the best of the genre is known for – when you’ve got skyscraper-sized lizards slugging it out MMA-style?

It is under these circumstances – or should I say restrictions? – that Godzilla Minus Zero enters the ring. As the sequel to the much-praised from three years ago – a picture that dealt with, among other things, notions of survivor’s guilt, hope in the face of hopelessness, found family, and more – Minus Zero is on the ropes from the start. Can returning writer-director Takashi Yamazaki wring even more out of his characters, who have already been to hell and back, while also blowin’ up stuff real good? In a word, no.

The film takes place two years after the events of Minus One, with Ryunosuke Kamiki back as Kōichi Shikishima and Minami Hamabe returning as Noriko. Kōichi, as fans of the Oscar-winning previous movie (for Best Visual Effects) will remember, is the former would-be kamikaze pilot from World War II who was instrumental in defeating Godzilla the first time around. Now married to Noriko, the woman he took in after the American air raids on Tokyo, the pair have also adopted Akiko, the orphaned baby they had cared for after that same disaster. Living happily together as a family, there’s only one thing that can ruin this idyllic picture… well, two things, since not only is Godzilla of course back, but there’s a new monster on the scene as well.

Minus Zero opens with a sequence of devastation, as this new critter lays waste to countless helpless civilians as they flee in the streets, avoiding both falling rubble from the buildings crumbling around them and lightning breath from the creature’s mouth. Yes, as fans have already figured out and as the marketing for the film has teased, this is Ghidorah, also known as King Ghidorah in the larger Toho mythology, and generally the archnemesis of the big guy for whom we have all gathered once again. (Ghidorah has also been referred to as “Monster Zero,” which helps to explain this film’s title.)

The scenes of destruction and terror are breathtaking.

These scenes of destruction and terror are breathtaking, with Yamazaki and his team of visual effects maestros once again managing to keep their creatures from feeling like CGI monstrosities. No, rather, Ghidorah, and Godzilla when he eventually shows up too, just appear to be monstrosities – humongous, slow-moving, reptile-like, and all-the more terrifying for it. Ghidorah also distinguishes himself from his counterpart with his scary yet herky-jerky, almost cat-like mannerisms.

So as soon as that first-round bell rings, the movie has already proven its VFX bona fides – to no one’s surprise. But it has also confirmed that a Godzilla Part 2 inevitably means more monsters. And look, none of this is to say that there’s anything wrong with a movie where Godzilla has to rip his own arm off because his foe’s teeth are sunk so tightly into it. We all love monster-on-monster action, but there’s no denying that the more of a mash a monster movie becomes – be it of the Toho, Universal, Alien/Xenomorph, or whatever else variety – the more it loses its edge as the human characters and their emotional baggage run the risk of looking puny in the face of these god-like creatures.

Remember what Bogart said in Casablanca? “It doesn't take much to see that the problems of three little people don't amount to a hill of beans in this crazy world.” Yes, I’m quoting Humphrey Bogart in a Godzilla review, but if there’s an issue with Minus Zero, it’s that the travails of Kōichi, Noriko, and little Akiko just pale when considering the scope of destruction that Godzilla and company are capable of. Whereas the first film framed that destruction through the lens of the trio’s trauma, not just in regards to the giant monster but also specifically around what they went through in the war, that resonance is missing here.

In fact, the most interesting character in Minus Zero is perhaps the most under-served. Kanji Murakami, played by Min Tanaka, is a scientist whose work is key to battling the monsters this time around. He’s also kind of warped, with Tanaka getting one scene in particular that is a bit too spoilery to describe here, but is also a highlight of the film. As with Kōichi and Noriko, and indeed every character in the film, the war irrevocably changed his life, and the scientist is still struggling to cope with that reality while he works to prevent a pair of living A-bombs from doing even more damage to humankind.

Speaking of which, a much ballyhooed sequence first glimpsed in the trailer last spring involving Godzilla and the Statue of Liberty is certainly something to behold here. Toho has asked critics to not reveal the specifics of this particular scene in reviews, but suffice to say that it is both everything you’ve imagined and theorized about, and at the same time none of that at all. It does connect back to Tanaka’s character in one of his darkest moments, and as a result is one of the film’s most memorable incidents of Godzilla-on-human action.

But that brings me back once again to the feeling that kept bubbling up for me while watching Godzilla Minus Zero. Even as Godzilla sets upon what looks like Spider-Noir’s version of New York City, the whole emotional underpinning of the scene is tied to Tanaka’s Murakami. Unfortunately, the character’s true motivations and how they’re ultimately resolved in the film play as more of an after-thought than Minus Zero’s thematic or emotional core, and for that film suffers.

If there is a central theme at work here, it’s the idea that no matter how hard we as a species try, we can’t outrun our own mistakes – and we’re gonna keep making them over and over again, despite the efforts of the best among us. Minus One ended with a hint of what was next for Noriko; while she miraculously survived a Godzilla attack, she also now bore a mysterious scar on her neck from the experience. It’s no surprise to learn in Minus Zero that it was no mere scar, and that in fact Noriko is now also a very important player in the fight against the monsters. But she, like Kōichi, is also a pawn in a greater game that’s happening on the world stage involving the monsters. The regular folks on the ground are the ones bearing the trauma of the battles that have been fought, but the powers that be don’t seem to care…

By the final act, you know where this is all going, and that’s fine. Monsters must brawl, and as with Minus One, the period setting of this film really adds to the luster of the visual effects and action scenes. Seeing Kōichi back in the pilot seat, this time of 1949-era fighter planes, is thrilling, and the various schemes concocted by the returning Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), now the head of the “Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau,” are often ingenious and satisfyingly crunchy in their attempts to slow down and ultimately stop Godzilla and his enemy.

items.title: Unabomber Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Unabomber covers the formative years and later arrest of Ted Kaczynski, the titular mail bomber who terrorized the US from the late 1970s until the mid-1990s. Director Janus Metz’s mixed bag of a film aims to understand the origin of a domestic terrorist but it never quite convinces or connects.

As FBI Agent Joanne Miller, Shailene Woodley — decent in a two-dimensional role almost any actress could have played — leads the surprisingly inert 1990s portions of the film chronicling the manhunt for Kaczynski, then a hermit living in the woods of Montana.

This storyline strives for serial killer movie suspense, but it never musters enough thrills to overcome its inherent tropes. It reduces the FBI’s capture of Kaczynski to a dull TV cop procedural instead of capturing the magnitude of what was a historic win for law enforcement.

What sets Unabomber apart from other projects about this notorious criminal are the portions set at Harvard University during the Cold War. This is where teenage Theodore Kaczynski (Jacob Tremblay), a brilliant mathematics student who yearns to be a philosopher, participates in a harrowing psychological experiment overseen by Professor Henry Murray (Russell Crowe).

Murray’s (now clearly unethical) program was meant to stress-test a person’s philosophical arguments, but instead it became an abusive quest to break a person until they changed. (It’s all very .)

The movie suggests that Murray ultimately unleashed a monster within Kaczynski who would later target the industrial and academic institutions he blamed for ruining the natural world and robbing humans of liberty. The reality is more complicated.

As the prodigy-era Kaczynski, Tremblay, try as he might, struggles to convey the psychological layers of his damaged character. Crowe delivers a fine but rote turn as the doctor who manipulated his student.

Murray’s actions certainly make him the heavy of this film, but Crowe plays him with enough haughtiness to prevent the character from being a complete mad scientist cliché. Like Kaczynski, Murray wants the world to know how brilliant he is but he may, in fact, just be a big loser.

If you’re on Netflix looking for something worth your while about this subject the better choice to stream would be the 2020 documentary Unabomber: In His Own Words.

items.title: We Build LEGO Mayor Manor: A Spooky, Not-So-Scary Halloween Build
items.author: Chris Reed
items.content:
The Mayor Manor, out now, is the theme's debut set (see it at Amazon). It's an engaging, enjoyable build, with a cool visual motif for LEGO to elaborate upon in the years to come.

The Mayor Manor is not ; it is open in the back like a classic dollhouse, allowing the builder to observe and stage the interior to his or her liking. It comes in nine bags – paper rather than plastic, thanks to LEGO's ongoing sustainability initiative. The switchover has been gradual, starting in 2020 and ramping up considerably in the last two years or so.

[A note about the paper bags: Make sure you shake and flatten them out completely before discarding them. Paper is not as slippery as plastic (nor as see-thru), and so if you're missing a piece, it might be stuck in the scraps. It happened to me twice during this build.]

The design is very '90s Tim-Burton-meets-Addams-Family. You have traditional spires mixed with stained glass windows, along with a foreboding gargoyle perched on the roof. The tree leaves are off-color blue and green, which creates the impression that you're viewing this house in the twilight rather than the bright light of day.

The house interior is well-appointed, featuring a fireplace which functionally connects to the house chimney on the exterior – a nice bit of logical, functional coherency. On the second floor, there's a grandfather clock with a golden pendulum and a face stuck at midnight. There's also a bookshelf, with the books inserted at various depths, which gives the space a bit of quirk and whimsy. If you enjoy putting together little builds, which you then insert, as furniture or other knick-knacks, into a larger build to create a whole? Then you'll really enjoy what's going on here.

The designers draw a clear line of distinction between the of the house, versus the house . The house has structural integrity; it's a two-story, traditionally built structure with defined rooms, level floors, and straight lines. But the facade of the house – the way it presents itself externally – is skewed, as if it's actively falling apart. LEGO accomplishes this by clipping crooked walls and roofs onto the underlying building. It's a convincing visual effect that'll make you do a double take.

Because half of the house appears destroyed and half appears relatively intact, we can imagine, in our mind's eye, how the house once appeared when it was whole. And it's especially cool to contrast that to the ruined state of the house, and see how this jagged split in the wall over here matches – like a high-concept jigsaw puzzle – to the broken wall over there.

Have you ever seen Ripley's Believe it or Not! museums in tourist areas? They're these self-billed "Odditoriums" that capitalize, P.T. Barnum style, on the off-beat and strange: "Come see a real shrunken head!" "Gaze upon an Iron Maiden torture device from medieval times!" "Young lady, have you ever laid eyes on a two-headed goat?"

I used to love these museums growing up, and I especially loved looking at their optical illusion facades from streetview, which made them appear as if they were sinking into the ground or experiencing the aftershocks of an earthquake. The closer I walked, the less convincing the illusion. But that also taught me something about myself – that knowing the 'trick' behind these illusions deepened my love for them rather than diminishing it.

I thought about this while putting together the Mayor Manor, particularly its East Wing. LEGO tells a story through its presentation; a stubborn intrusive tree has grown into the house's foundations, and over time, it's punctured through the walls and wrapped itself around half of the second floor. It implies that the house is very, very old, but also that the inhabitants of the house – the pale-faced matron with the fur-lined shawl, and the maid and butler who wait upon her – are either indifferent to what's happening or are unable to prevent it.

Are they ghosts or the undead? Were they once inhabitants of this house when they were alive? How long have they roamed these hallways in the years since? They don't look unhappy, strictly speaking.

This sort of imaginative "what-if?" roleplay is essential, I think, to your full enjoyment of adult-geared sets like these. Because unlike many other 18+ sets, this is not a painstaking replica or a pop culture artifact; this is a playset, with the dimensions and features of one. Children have the ability to construct elaborate play scenarios—a skill we often lose as we grow older. LEGO sets like these give adults tacit permission to indulge in those joys once more.

But even if you don't have the suspension of disbelief to throw yourself into fantasy entirely, there is still childish joy and escapism in imagining the inner lives of these minifigures, and in staging dramatic scenarios when putting them out for display.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas – The Legacy Review
items.author: Luke Reilly
items.content:
I’m taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t come with any new IGN score, but they will re-examine what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release. By the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly rank in my long-term love for this series.

Today it’s time to go home to Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas.

Whether you remember it or not – or were too preoccupied being spoon-fed puréed fruit from a jar at the time – it’s impossible to understate what a banner year 2004 was for now-legendary video games. Just look at the line up. World of Warcraft. Half-Life 2 and Halo 2. Burnout 3 and Metal Gear Solid 3. Gran Turismo 4 and more – much more. I could absolutely go on. To emerge as the bestselling game of what may well be the greatest year we’ve ever had – in an era where it felt like the rulebook was being torn up and rewritten every other month – you had to be remarkable. You had to be rich, surprising, innovative, and essential. Simply put, to be the bestselling game of 2004, you needed to be more than great. You needed to be Grand.

While GTA III defined the fundamentals of 3D open-world design, and Vice City layered that sandbox with vibrant ’80s style and a big dose of yacht rock and yayo, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas pushed the formula to the very limits of what was actually possible on the world’s then-favourite DVD player. Despite shipping just two years after Vice City, San Andreas expanded Rockstar’s formula exponentially by introducing full-scale cities – all housed in what amounted to an entire fictional US state: the titular San Andreas. Best of all, it was still retro-tinged, set in 1992. A slightly less dramatic leap into the past than Vice City but, as someone whose adolescence was forged in the ’90s, an awesome period to revisit.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas pushed the formula to the very limits of what was actually possible on the world’s then-favourite DVD player.

At the time, it was a mindblowing achievement. The state itself covers an area roughly six times larger than Vice City. Its three major metropolises – Los Santos, San Fierro, and Las Venturas – each have their own unique visual identity. Los Santos is draped in smog, giving the whole cityscape a distinct orange haze at certain times of day. On the hottest days, a shimmering heat rises from the asphalt – a fabulously effective flourish that gives the city a truly tangible sense of temperature. San Fierro, defined by its severe hills and stretches of tramline, features an entirely different sort of climate. It’s more akin to GTA III’s Liberty City, where the tall, dense skyscrapers of the CBD create quite a bit of shade below. Las Venturas, San Andreas’ gambling haven, is dry, flat, and is at its best at neon-lit night. Each city is connected by open stretches of rolling fields, redwood forests, and rocky desert. There’s even a selection of tiny towns, farms, and factories between the major hubs.

However, while the size of the map was one thing – the fact that you can travel all over it and move from one major city to another without a single loading screen is something else altogether. Coming from Vice City, where you couldn’t cross from one island to the other without being briefly stalled by a loading screen, it was a genuinely amazing advancement. Rockstar had concocted a way to constantly stream in the world immediately around us in real-time. For its debut on PS2 – the platform that accounted for more than 17 million of San Andreas’ 27.5 million sales – this meant a neverending juggling act with the system’s limited 32MB of RAM and a relentless assault on its disc drive. You probably could’ve forgiven the Rockstar North team for adding a high-speed fighter jet to a game perpetually pulling data from its dual-layer DVD in a non-stop race against time to rapidly build the world in front of you before you reached it.

It’s arguable San Andreas’ greatest victory isn’t simply the immense geographical scale it boasted for its era. Rather, it’s the remarkable density of its various systems, ideas, and side activities.

I played an aggressive amount of San Andreas back in the mid 2000s. I tortured my PS2 until it started making weird noises, then I borrowed my sister’s and tortured it, too. Perhaps the ultimate testament to how supremely stuffed San Andreas is with things to do is just how many side modes I’ve encountered over the last week of playing that had honestly slipped my mind over the last 20 years. The valet activity? Forgot that. Trucking missions? Forgot those. Duelling lowriders? Oh, yeah! It’s like putting on an old pair of trousers and finding $20 notes in every pocket.

San Andreas almost never stops giving.

San Andreas almost never stops giving. Take its vehicles, for instance. Not only do they all handle with a genuine sense of heft that puts most GTA clones to shame – seriously, just watch as they subtly wiggle on their springs if you jerk them to a sudden halt – but there are also around 200 of them. From the minute it puts you on a bicycle, new vehicles are in virtually constant supply. Combine harvesters. Quad bikes. Articulated semi-trailers. Monster trucks. Functional forklifts. Hovercraft. A jump jet, a jetpack. No, not one or the other. Both. It’s like someone took a bunch of scribbled brainstorm notes and executed on every suggestion, without trimming any of them.

To be honest, there are times playing San Andreas where it almost feels like no idea was trimmed. Rob a house, go dancing, and stop at a minimart to play an arcade machine. Hit the gym, then hit the casino. Run a triathlon, and run a business. Go parachuting, unwind with some pool, and… role play as a pimp. I guess, strictly speaking, there was at least one idea that famously pulled out at the last minute: a sex minigame. It just wasn’t pulled out enough, so to speak. Ruled out so late in development it was impractical to completely remove it without jeopardising San Andreas’ vast, precarious, and otherwise interwoven code, Rockstar locked off the minigame beneath a non-interactive wrapper – keeping the camera entirely out of the room where the magic was happening. Modders discovered and re-enabled it in time for the PC version in 2005, triggering what became known as the Hot Coffee controversy.

The pearl clutching and hand wringing that followed was deeply embarrassing, even by mid 2000s standards. The US ESRB re-issued all versions of the game a commercially crippling Adults Only rating, and Australia temporarily banned it until the abandoned content was removed. It didn’t matter that it literally wasn’t even accessible for the majority of players on console – the matter had become politicised and the subject of massive media attention. The concept of two blocky PS2 characters goofily grinding against each other was apparently too much for adult gamers to bear. We would have to be content with wanton vehicular homicide and burning cops to a crisp. I’m hopeful that things would go a little differently more than two decades on, but I guess we have our own problems. These days I don’t know if I’m still killing people in video games, or if I’m only unaliving them.

The explosion of side activities is still only part of the San Andreas equation, as Rockstar also introduced a number of light RPG mechanics. This goes beyond the ability to customise leading man Carl Johnson’s appearance, via outfits, haircuts, tattoos, or munching down too many burgers. CJ also has a large number of improveable skills, and the more you do something, the better and more efficient he’ll get at it. Flying, fighting, driving, diving – you name it. Have a weapon you prefer? Use it as much as possible to level CJ up to ‘Hitman’ proficiency, where you can move and strafe while shooting, your lock-on range will extend, and (in the case of the four specific weapons) even dual wield them.

The improvements to the third-person shooter component in San Andreas are significant, with most of the clumsiness that tended to characterise GTA III and Vice City ironed out. A bulk of that is thanks to the ability to finally use the right analogue stick to control the camera at will – as opposed to the previous games, where the right stick was only used to look around in a stationary first-person camera. It’s the first GTA game to feel akin to a modern third-person shooter in this regard, which makes it a breeze to get accustomed to in 2026. You can also aim all weapons freely now, rather than just a select few – and the auto lock-on is otherwise intelligent enough to automatically prioritise and target threats rather than random civilians or, worse, your own gang members. Light stealth was even introduced, on the back of Rockstar’s own experimentation with the controversial Manhunt earlier the same year. CJ is able to crouch to reduce noise, a suppressed pistol has been added to the arsenal, and there’s a simple stealth kill you can perform on the unaware, indicated by the same raised-arm trigger used in Manhunt.

With more cities, more cars, and more depth than ever, you might have been wondering just how much more San Andreas could possibly have in store.

Well, I haven’t even touched on the radio stations yet, which are neck and neck with Vice City as the best they’ve ever been in the 30-year history of the series. It’s an impeccably curated soundtrack that’s one part perfect ’90s time capsule, and one part historical hip hop odyssey. That is, it didn’t just feature some of the most iconic rap tracks to emerge from the early ’90s, but it made sure to include stations dedicated to the entire ecosystem of complementary music hip hop found itself drawing inspiration from. Funk and soul. R&B and New Jack Swing. There’s perhaps no better example of that than the fact San Andreas didn’t make a choice between Charles Wright’s signature hit Express Yourself, or the 1988 reimaging from N.W.A. It simply included both. Eleven stations and over 150 songs is the bullet point, but there’s so much more to it than that. It’s the fact that they now air dynamically, meaning the song order changes and you won’t always hear the same slice of DJ banter introducing them.

Want more? Well, how about arguably the greatest arsenal of cheats codes ever assembled? Cheats to make the game easier. Cheats to make the game harder. Cheats to spawn all the greatest vehicles. Cheats to arm civilians with rocket launchers. Cheats to trigger a map-wide riot. Cheats to turn off the gravity!

want more? How about a same screen co-op mode that allows you to bring a friend into the world to wreak havoc alongside you. Is it slightly janky? Yes. Did that stop my friends and I from messing around with it constantly? Absolutely not.

Interestingly, about the only thing San Andreas seems to have fewer of is major Hollywood celebrities in the main roles. Following Vice City, San Andreas moved away from having a big-shot celebrity on deck to star as the lead character. Instead, CJ was capably and memorably played by an LA-based rapper named Young Maylay, with no previous acting experience. There are a number of recognisable names here as side characters, though, including James Woods, Peter Fonda, Charlie Murphy, Ice-T, Chris Penn, and the inimitable Sam Jackson as the iconically slimy Officer Frank Tenpenny. Is there a better GTA villain than Jackson’s Tenpenny? I don’t think there is.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas is the single bestselling game on the most successful console in the history of the business. That’s not an accolade you can just earn by accident. Its unprecedented scope and astonishing depth were nothing short of witchcraft, and the incredible attention to detail was staggeringly impressive for something of its size. Its ability to support endless experimentation kept my friends and I busy for years, fooling around with its industry-leading list of cheats and its same-screen co-op chaos long after we’d all finished the story mode several times. Its soundtrack is the stuff of legend; so one-of-a-kind that not even Rockstar itself could quite reassemble the complete thing for subsequent re-releases. In 2004, GTA San Andreas was one of the most extraordinary games I’d ever played. In 2026, the hood done took me under all over again. Sure, the technical limitations of the mid 2000s are always obvious through a modern lens, but you can’t measure ambition in polygons – and GTA San Andreas is overflowing with it.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

items.title: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
This review currently only covers Ace Combat 8's single-player campaign, as reviewers were given a very limited amount of time with its multiplayer modes ahead of release. It will be updated with a finalized score and multiplayer impressions once we put the PvP through its paces on live servers.

There’s a theory that it’s impossible to make a piece of anti-war art set during a war – that, no matter what you do, the work itself inevitably becomes (or will be interpreted as) pro-war. I’m sympathetic to the argument; Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve is a war story about how awesome it is to be a heroic ace pilot. It is also unapologetically anti-war and plays with complex ideas like the role of propaganda, the power of symbols, nationalism and globalism. And it extends to the way corporations influence and manipulate world events, social media and the rise of news that may or may not be real, the price and horrors of war, and what a world without borders might look like. Its story is often startlingly relevant, but when I think about my time with it, my mind returns to a single thought: Wings of Theve’s never directly stated but deeply held belief that the best thing that could happen to this world and its characters would be for the war to be over, and for none of them to ever fly a combat mission again. It marries exceptional air combat with a melodramatic but moving story, one of the year’s best soundtracks, and incredible visual design to make a war game that never lets you forget how terrible everything happening here is.

Wings of Theve takes place about ten years after Ace Combat 7, though you don’t need to be familiar with its predecessor to enjoy it. The Republic of Sotoa launches a blitzkrieg invasion of the Federation of Central Usea using the power of its air force and orbital missiles strikes known as Tonitrus Spears. The FCU capital of Theve falls. Shattered and broken, what’s left of the FCU fights a hopeless, defensive war from the deck of the Endurance, an aging aircraft carrier that, in better times, would have probably ended up as a museum, but the crew of the Endurance fights on. Your character, a nameless fighter pilot, is fished out of the ocean by one of the Endurance’s rescue helicopters, and you’re quickly assigned to fly second seat to Jan “Rex” Cope, the legendary Wings of Theve, the FCU’s ace of aces.

Trouble is, it’s all a lie. Cope is an exceptional pilot, but he’s never shot anyone down. His kill count is a myth, fabricated to give the people of Usea hope. As long as the Wings of Theve is in the skies, the story goes, the fight isn’t over. Cope’s job is to bring his squadron, Joker Flight, back with him. And he’s done it well. But his luck runs out when you run into Sotoan ace Shadow 22. But the Wings of Theve cannot die, so you inherit the mantle and Cope’s old callsign. You have become the name. And when legend becomes fact, print the legend and watch it go viral on social media. But it’s not enough for Joker Flight to just run anymore. They need to produce results. And as you start to shoot down enemy fighters, the lines between the legend of the Wings of Theve and reality start to blur.

It’s a compelling yarn that developer Project Aces has spun, and it unravels into an earnest story with the Joker Flight crew at its heart. Baxter (callsign “Professor”) is a former teacher turned pilot, mentor to the other members of Joker Flight, and your wingman; Tasha, Joker Flight’s youngest member, a generationally-talented civvie stunt pilot forced into service by the war who refuses to shoot anyone down; and Coster (callsign “Noise”), a quiet rock and roll enthusiast who manages to fly Tasha’s wing while blasting tunes over your comms. Many other supporting characters feed into the myth of the Wings of Theve whether it be your commanding XO, your Queen Flight counterparts, or the media machine spinning you up. And through it all, the legend of Cope (and his spirit) lingers.

Make no mistake, it is Wings of Theve’s characters that make this story work.

Maybe that sounds silly, but like everything else in Wings of Theve, it works surprisingly well and allows you to continue to build a connection to a character whose life and death are crucial to Wings of Theve’s world. And make no mistake, it is Wings of Theve’s characters that make this story work. They’re well-drawn, complex, interesting people elevated by genuinely excellent performances from the voice cast and your relationships with these characters drive much of Wings of Theve’s story. Whenever we sortied, I wanted to make sure I brought them home.

Ace Combat has long told its story from inside the cockpit, but Wings of Theve also puts your character on the Endurance’s deck, inside the mess with your fellow pilots and civvies who have sought refuge on the carrier, and inside hangars briefing rooms, among other places. These moments help you connect with the members of Joker Flight and the other people aboard the Endurance, but they also drive home the cost of the war, and make it feel like this world exists outside of the cockpit. You can’t really do much during them except look around and perform simple interactions, but they're home to some of Wings of Theve’s most memorable and affecting moments.

Ultimately, though, you’re a combat pilot; your place is in the air. And it’s here that Ace Combat soars (sorry), expertly weaving its story, moment-to-moment gameplay, and mission design into masterful, elegant maneuvers worthy of a state-of-the-art fighter jet. Like its predecessors, Wings of Theve is a mission-based game. After you’ve been briefed on your next sortie, you’ll select your aircraft, weapons, and parts – which you can buy (along with new planes) with points you earn by completing missions. All that affects everything from how many missiles or special weapons you can equip or how much damage they do to how well your plane handles. You can even outfit your crew’s planes if you want (or have them auto-assigned something that fits the mission at hand). Then you’re airborne, and it’s time to fly.

Often, things start pretty simply. Maybe you need to defend the Endurance, assault an air field, protect a friendly plane, or take out some transports. But these initial objectives are just a reason to take to the air. The beauty of Ace Combat has always been in its flying, when the infinite possibilities of the skies above intersect with the limitations of your aircraft and the realities of your mission. You could play with the standard controls, which substantially limit your aircraft, but you should absolutely play with the Expert scheme if you can. The joy lives in the complete control of the pitch, roll, and yaw of your plane, simultaneously opening you to rapturous moments of aviation choreography and shattering mistakes when you misjudge a turn or your altitude resulting in a devastating crash.

You find yourself in small moments: in the high-G turns to evade incoming missiles, locking onto a group of planes with a special anti-air weapon and knocking four of them out of the sky at once, or deftly weaving through a city and over debris. Wings of Theve captures the fighter pilot fantasy when you're getting on a target's six and downing them with a perfectly placed series of machine gun shots or in finding just the right air speed to stay behind a massive transport before turning your nose and shredding its engines with your guns without ever firing a missile.

It expertly weaves its story, gameplay, and mission design together.
